# Lairy — full reference

> Lairy is a design system with the visual language of an operator console: dark-first, monospaced, amber-accented, with a locked 2px corner.

# Tokens

## Surface

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | dark `#07090b` · light `#f3f4f5` | Page background. | — | — |
| `--glow` | dark `rgba(150, 165, 175, 0.10)` · light `rgba(120, 135, 145, 0.12)` | The ambient radial-gradient tint behind the workspace header. | — | Not part of the prototype's own dsTokens() catalogue table — added for the workspace header's ambient background effect, which the documented Color foundation page predates. Themeable because, like every other Surface tint, it is expressed as a low-opacity value over the ground and must invert with it (colorContent's alpha-over-ground rule). |
| `--panel` | dark `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.02)` · light `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.02)` | Card fill. | — | — |
| `--panel-2` | dark `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.045)` · light `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.05)` | Hover / active fill. | A second, alternate card style — it is reserved for the state a pointer or a selection put there, a response rather than a style choice (colorDocs "Surface" role). | — |

## Line

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--border` | dark `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.16)` · light `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2)` | Hairline, dividers. | — | — |
| `--border-2` | dark `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.28)` · light `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.32)` | Emphasis border. | — | — |
| `--bracket` | dark `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.45)` · light `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.45)` | HUD corner brackets. | An ordinary divider or emphasis edge — it is the HUD corner mark only (colorDocs "Line" role); use --border or --border-2 instead. | — |

## Text

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--dim` | dark `#c6ced6` · light `#333c45` | Secondary text. | — | — |
| `--faint` | dark `#7c8791` · light `#767f88` | Tertiary only — never body. | Body text or a sentence — it is the only text rank that does not clear AA for body copy in either theme, legal only on counters, timestamps and single-word meta (colorA11y "Faint is a caption colour"). A sentence set in it is a bug. | — |
| `--fg` | dark `#f2f5f8` · light `#0e1216` | Primary text, icons. | — | — |
| `--mute` | dark `#9aa5b0` · light `#586269` | Labels, timestamps. | — | — |

## Accent

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--accent` | dark `#f7bd63` · light `#9a6208` | Live, alert, primary action. | A second, simultaneous focus in the same view — if two elements are amber, neither reads as the answer; demote the weaker one instead (colorContent). | — |
| `--accent-line` | dark `rgba(247, 189, 99, 0.5)` · light `rgba(154, 98, 8, 0.42)` | Accent border. | — | — |
| `--accent-soft` | dark `rgba(247, 189, 99, 0.16)` · light `rgba(154, 98, 8, 0.1)` | Accent fill. | — | — |

## Accent — secondary (Ice)

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--accent-2` | dark `#7fd8ff` · light `#0d6d92` | Secondary signal — data, links in charts, informational state. | Something clickable that amber is not already leading — Ice refers, it never leads an action on its own (colorDocs "Ice" role). | — |
| `--accent-2-line` | dark `rgba(127, 216, 255, 0.5)` · light `rgba(13, 109, 146, 0.42)` | Secondary border. | — | — |
| `--accent-2-soft` | dark `rgba(127, 216, 255, 0.16)` · light `rgba(13, 109, 146, 0.1)` | Secondary fill. | — | — |

## Alarm

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--alarm` | #ff8f6b | Failure, and only failure. | Anything that is not a failure state — no theme may redefine what "broken" looks like, and nothing may borrow the colour by accident. | Failure, and only failure. It is written literally rather than tokenised on purpose: a theme should never be able to redefine what broken looks like, and nothing should be able to borrow the colour by accident. |
| `--alarm-ink` | #07090b | Text and icon colour for content set on a solid --alarm fill — the primary action button on a Warning or Error tone. | Anything not sitting on a solid --alarm fill — for a failure-tinted border or wash, use --alarm-line or --alarm-soft against the ordinary text ranks instead. | Failure, and only failure. It is written literally rather than tokenised on purpose: a theme should never be able to redefine what broken looks like, and nothing should be able to borrow the colour by accident. Not itself in the prototype: renderCallout() used var(--bg) for text on a solid alarm fill, which fails AA in the light theme (2.03:1) because --bg is themeable but --alarm is not. --alarm-ink is proposed to close that gap and, for the same reason as --alarm itself, is non-themeable — a themeable ink colour paired with a non-themeable fill would drift out of contrast in exactly one theme. |
| `--alarm-line` | rgba(255, 143, 107, 0.4) | Failure-state border, reduced opacity — e.g. Callout and Toast's Warning/Error border. | — | Failure, and only failure. It is written literally rather than tokenised on purpose: a theme should never be able to redefine what broken looks like, and nothing should be able to borrow the colour by accident. |
| `--alarm-soft` | rgba(255, 143, 107, 0.1) | Failure-state fill, low opacity — e.g. Callout's Error tone background. | — | Failure, and only failure. It is written literally rather than tokenised on purpose: a theme should never be able to redefine what broken looks like, and nothing should be able to borrow the colour by accident. |

## Typography — family

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--font-body` | 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace | Body copy, the system default.; Body, Small, Label, Micro and the document default (typoTokens). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--font-heading` | 'Space Grotesk', sans-serif | Headings and titles.; Display, Title and Metric — weight 600 only (typoTokens). | Body copy, labels or anything set at Section size or smaller. | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |

## Typography — weight

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--weight-regular` | 400 | Every IBM Plex Mono style — Body, Small, Label, Micro. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--weight-semibold` | 600 | Every Space Grotesk style — Display, Title, Metric, Section — and nothing else. | A one-off emphasis inside body copy — "weight is fixed": the scale changes size and tracking to make a point, it never reaches for a weight (typoScaleNotes). | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |

## Typography — size

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--text-body` | 14px | Rows, paragraphs (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--text-callout-title` | 14.5px | Callout's title text. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). Harvested from the prototype's own renderCallout() rather than the documented six-step scale — it lands between Small (13) and Section (17), where the scale has no step. Reviewed and kept as a component-specific size in the LDS-012 token decisions pass. |
| `--text-display` | 48px | Page hero only (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--text-doc-title` | 34px | Docs page title (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--text-label` | 12px | Uppercase panel headers, chips (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--text-metric` | 28px | Numbers in stat cards (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--text-micro` | 11px | Uppercase codes, badges, table headers (docs/prd.md §8.2). | Anything smaller — this is the hard floor. Nothing in Lairy is set below Micro (AGENTS.md rule 6, docs/prd.md §8.2). | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--text-section` | 17px | Section titles (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |

| `--text-title` | 28px | Workspace name (docs/prd.md §8.2). | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |

## Typography — leading

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--leading-body` | 1.6 | Paired with --text-body for rows and paragraphs. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--leading-callout-title` | 1.2 | Paired with --text-callout-title for Callout's title. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). Not specified in the prototype's inline style for renderCallout() — a browser's normal line-height for a single-line 600-weight label is roughly 1.2. Harvested as a proposed value in the LDS-012 token decisions pass rather than left unset. |
| `--leading-display` | 1.08 | Paired with --text-display for the page hero style. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--leading-doc-title` | 1.1 | Paired with --text-doc-title for the docs page title. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--leading-label` | 1.4 | Paired with --text-label for uppercase panel headers and chips. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--leading-metric` | 1.1 | Paired with --text-metric for stat-card numerals. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--leading-micro` | 1.4 | Paired with --text-micro for uppercase codes, badges and table headers. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |
| `--leading-section` | 1.3 | Paired with --text-section for section titles. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). docs/prd.md §8.2 leaves Section's leading as "per prototype" with no fixed figure: the prototype's section-title spans set no line-height at all (browser default), while its one wrapped use — the docs page's opening sentence — used 1.55. 1.3 is a harvested middle value serving both, flagged in the LDS-012 token decisions pass. |
| `--leading-small` | 1.5 | Paired with --text-small for module titles, hints, buttons and card body. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). The Typography foundation's own documented value. The prototype's Callout body used 1.55; documented foundations win over prototype markup where they disagree (ADR-0005), so 1.5 is used here and the difference is flagged rather than silently reconciled. |
| `--leading-title` | 1.15 | Paired with --text-title for the workspace name. | — | A typographic value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.2). |

## Spacing

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--space-12` | 12px | Rows inside a group, grid gaps in a legend or a small card set. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-16` | 16px | Vertical inset of a panel, and the gap between unrelated blocks inside one card. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-18` | 18px | Horizontal inset of a panel. Paired with 16 vertical so text clears the corner without looking centred. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-22` | 22px | Inset of a large tile, where the content is a heading rather than a row. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-32` | 32px | Between numbered sections of a page, and between major regions of a workspace. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-4` | 4px | A label and the value it names. The smallest distance in the system, and the only one that still reads as one thing. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-44` | 44px | Page-level breathing room: under a page header, around a hero, at the outer gutter. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). docs/prd.md §8.3's prose names eight steps (4–32); the prototype's own spacingDocs() ramp and reference/harvest-tokens.mjs's SPACING_RAMP already treat 44 as a ninth step, with real padding/margin occurrences mapped onto it, so it is included here rather than left as an off-ramp value (LDS-012). |
| `--space-6` | 6px | Icon to its text inside a control, and the gap between stacked lines of a caption. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |
| `--space-8` | 8px | Sibling controls in a row — buttons, chips, a field and its adornment. | — | A spacing value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.3). |

## Radius

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--radius` | 2px | Every surface — the .ds lock. | Nesting inside another rounded container — radii do not nest, so rows, dividers and headers inside a rounded panel stay square and run edge to edge (radiusContent).; Scaling with the size of the box — a 900px modal and a 20px badge share the same corner (radiusContent). | A radius value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.4). Enforced in code via .ds's border-radius 2px !important, not by convention. |
| `--radius-chip` | 20px | Chips only. | A size — it is a shape token, not part of the radius scale, and stays 20px at every chip height so the ends always read as fully round (radiusContent). | A radius value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.4). |

## Icon

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--icon-callout` | 17px | Callout's icon width and height (17×17), harvested from the prototype's calloutIcon(). | — | A dimension, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary. It predates the Icons foundation size scale below and stays a standalone exception rather than being folded into it: 17px is Callout's own harvested value, not an instance of the Inline icon scale's 16px box. |
| `--icon-glyph-rail` | 22px | The Glyph box in the dock rail and other collapsed-nav contexts (Icons foundation, Glyph scale). | — | A dimension, not a colour — one value for both themes by design. The lower end of the Glyph scale's documented 22–34px range (icoDocs); packages/content/src/entries/foundations/icons.ts's own extractionNotes flagged this range as tokenless pending this ticket (LDS-017). |
| `--icon-glyph-tile` | 34px | The Glyph box for section tiles and empty states (Icons foundation, Glyph scale). | — | A dimension, not a colour — one value for both themes by design. The upper end of the Glyph scale's range and the prototype glyph()'s own default size; the Glyph React component (packages/ui/src/icons/glyph.tsx) defaults to this size. |
| `--icon-inline` | 16px | The Inline icon box (Icons foundation, Inline icon scale). | — | A dimension, not a colour — one value for both themes by design. Fixed rather than a range: the prototype's icon() hardcodes 16×16 with no size parameter, because the Inline icon scale is sized to match 14px body text rather than a rail/tile pair like Glyph. |
| `--icon-stroke-glyph` | 2.2 | Stroke width for every Glyph path (Icons foundation Construction rule 2). | — | A number, not a colour — one value for both themes by design; a stroke weight has no dark/light axis. Heavier than the inline stroke on purpose, per the Icons foundation: at 22px in a column of its own, a glyph has no adjacent type to borrow weight from. |
| `--icon-stroke-inline` | 2 | Stroke width for every Inline icon path (Icons foundation Construction rule 2). | — | A number, not a colour — one value for both themes by design. Sized and weighted to match 14px body text, which is why it looks thin if scaled up into Glyph territory. |

## Motion — easing

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--easing-draw` | cubic-bezier(.35, 0, .2, 1) | The blueprint line-draw curve, used only there. | Anything other than the blueprint line-draw. | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). |
| `--easing-standard` | cubic-bezier(.4, 0, .2, 1) | Panel and Reveal's curve — anything that changes shape or enters the page. | — | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). |
| `--easing-symmetric` | cubic-bezier(.45, 0, .55, 1) | The sweepline loop's curve. | — | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). |

## Motion — duration

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--duration-control` | 180ms | Buttons and inputs, where several properties change together: fill, border, transform and shadow. | — | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). |
| `--duration-instant` | 140ms | Hover fills, chip toggles, row highlights, the fade on a revealed action — short enough to feel like a property of the pointer rather than an animation. | — | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). |
| `--duration-panel` | 260ms | Anything that changes the shape of the page: the dock collapsing, the drawer taking width, the header sliding to follow. | — | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). |
| `--duration-reveal` | 500ms | Cards and panels arriving on first paint, spread 360–600ms with no delay on anything. | — | A motion value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.5). The prototype varies this 450–600ms per group weight; 500ms is the documented base step (Motion page motDocs). |

References the themed --accent token via color-mix so the tint follows theme, even though the shadow token itself is not per-theme. |

## Elevation — z-index

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--z-chrome` | 4 | The dock, the subnav rail and the top status bar — flat, and first. | — | An elevation value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.7). |
| `--z-command-bar` | 60 | Above the page and its chrome, below anything that could interrupt it. | — | An elevation value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.7). |
| `--z-overlay` | 80 | Modal and drawer — the blocking layer. Both live at the same stop because two are never open at once. | — | An elevation value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.7). |
| `--z-rail-stub` | 36 | The collapsed-rail handle — above chrome only because it sits on the seam between two pieces of it. | — | An elevation value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.7). |
| `--z-toast` | 90 | The top of the ladder, so a confirmation is legible over a modal that caused it. | A scrim — Toast is the one stop that never takes one, because a toast interrupts nothing (elevZ). | An elevation value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.7). |

## Breakpoint

| Token | Value | Use for | Never for | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--breakpoint-desktop` | 1024px | The desktop range starts here (1024–1439px) — the prototype's own minimum width. | — | A layout value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.6). |
| `--breakpoint-tablet` | 640px | The tablet range starts here (640–1023px); below it is phone, the unprefixed default. | — | A layout value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.6). |
| `--breakpoint-wide` | 1440px | The wide range starts here (≥1440px). | — | A layout value, not a colour — it holds one value for both themes by design; there is no dark/light axis to vary (docs/prd.md §8.6). |

# Components

## Badges

Status: stable · Version: 1.2.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/badge

Purpose: A small, square, system-assigned label stating a standing condition on a row. The operator cannot dismiss it.

### Description

A badge is a static label that reports the state of the thing it sits beside.

It is assigned by the system, never by the operator, and it is never clickable. The moment a badge can be pressed, filtered or dismissed it has become a Chip and belongs on that page instead. This is the one rule that keeps the two apart — everything below follows from it.

### Anatomy

1. Container — 1px hairline, 2px radius, transparent fill. Never a solid block — filled badges compete with buttons.
2. Label — 10.5px, uppercase, .12em tracking. One word where possible, two at most.
3. Padding — 2px vertical, 8px horizontal. Fixed — badges never grow to fill a column.
4. Parent — The row, card or title the badge annotates. A badge never floats free of one.

### Variants

- Neutral (--mute, --border): Classification with no judgement attached — origin, type, owner.
- Info (--accent-2, --accent-2-line): A fact worth noticing that needs no response.
- Success (--accent, --accent-line): A good terminal state — passed, approved, running.
- Fail (--alarm, --alarm-line): A bad terminal state. The only badge that may sit alone in a row.

There is no Warning tone. A state is either fine, notable, or broken — a fourth degree of alarm gets ignored along with the third.

### Use when

- The state is assigned by the system and the operator cannot change it directly.
- The state belongs to something else on screen — a row, a card, a title.
- It matters at a glance, scanned rather than read.
- The vocabulary is closed: a fixed set of words, not free text.

### Use something else when

- chip: It can be clicked, toggled or removed — that is a Chip.
- toast: It announces an event that just happened — that is a Toast.
- progress: It reports a quantity moving over time — that is Progress.

### Content rules

- Uppercase, 10.5px, .12em tracking. Never sentence case.
- One word wherever the language allows. Two is the ceiling; "PENDING REVIEW" is the longest badge in the system.
- State, not instruction. "FAILED", never "FIX THIS".
- No punctuation, no ellipsis, no counts inside the label — a count is its own component.
- The same state uses the same word everywhere. "LIVE" is never also "ACTIVE" or "RUNNING".

### Examples

- [demo] Neutral
- [demo] Info
- [demo] Success
- [demo] Fail
- [good] Badge beside its title — Badge annotates its parent, on the same baseline as the title.
- [bad] Three badges stacked — Never stack badges — if a row needs three, the row needs a column instead.
- [good] One-word label — One word, uppercase, no punctuation.
- [bad] A sentence as a label — Never a sentence. Badges are read at a glance, not parsed.
- [good] Colour plus word — Colour plus word. The word carries the meaning on its own.
- [bad] Colour alone — Never colour alone — a bare dot is unreadable to a third of operators.

### Accessibility

- Not focusable: A badge takes no tabindex and no role. It is text inside its parent, so a screen reader announces it as part of the row rather than as a separate stop.
- Never colour alone: Every badge carries a word. Tone reinforces the word; it never replaces it. This is what keeps the four tones legible under deuteranopia.
- Contrast: All four tones clear 4.5:1 against --panel in both themes. Fail is the tightest at 4.6:1 in light — do not tint it further.
- Reading order: The badge follows the title it modifies in source order, so the announcement reads "Normalize step, failed" rather than "failed, Normalize step".

### Tokens

- --mute, --border: Neutral tone
- --accent-2, --accent-2-line: Info tone
- --accent, --accent-line: Success tone
- --panel: Assumed backdrop for contrast

### Related

- chip (contrasts-with): Interactive and user-owned. If it can be clicked, filtered or dismissed, it is a chip.
- toast (often-confused-with): Same four intents, but transient and system-initiated. A badge persists; a toast interrupts.
- progress (alternative): Use when the state is a quantity over time rather than a name.

### Changelog

- v1.2.0 (16 Aug 2026): Tones realigned to the four Toast intents. Info moved to Ice.
- v1.1.0 (15 Aug 2026): Container radius locked to 2px with the system-wide sharp lock.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Initial release — four tones, label format only.

---

## Buttons

Status: stable · Version: 1.3.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/button

Purpose: Commits an action the operator has decided to take.

### Description

A button commits an action the operator has decided to take.

It changes something — runs, saves, deletes, confirms. If the control only changes what is shown, it is Tabs or a link, not a button; if it carries a value the operator picked rather than an action, it is a Chip. Everything below assumes the click has a consequence.

### Anatomy

1. Padding — 9px vertical, 16px horizontal on every variant, so a row of mixed buttons shares one height.
2. Label — 12.5px, 600 weight, .06em tracking, uppercase. A verb, never a noun.
3. Icon slot — Optional 14px leading glyph at 8px from the label. Trailing icons are reserved for menus and links.
4. Container — 1px border, 2px radius, 32px minimum height. The border is present on every variant except Ghost, which draws one on hover.

### Variants

- Primary (--accent, --bg): The one action the screen exists for. Never two on the same view — if two things look primary, neither is.
- Secondary (--border-2, --fg): A real alternative to the primary action: cancel, go back, pick the other path. Outlined, never filled.
- Ghost (--dim): Tertiary and repeated actions — toolbar controls, row actions, anything that would shout if it were bordered.
- Danger (--alarm-line, --alarm-soft, --fg): Destructive and irreversible only. Delete, revoke, purge. Never for "remove filter" or anything a click can undo.

There is no Link variant. A link navigates and belongs in prose; giving it a button shell teaches operators that the two behave alike, and then a misplaced click costs them work.

### States

- Default: At rest. Primary is the only variant carrying a fill.
- Hover: Fill lightens 22% and a soft lift shadow appears. 140ms.
- Active: Fill darkens 18%, the button drops 1px and the shadow inverts inward. No duration — it tracks the pointer.
- Focus: 3px --accent-soft ring plus an --accent-line border. Identical on every variant, including Danger.
- Disabled: 35% opacity, not-allowed cursor. Never removed from the DOM — a vanished button reads as a bug.

### Use when

- The click commits something — data is written, a job starts, a record is destroyed.
- The operator chose to act, rather than being told about something.
- The action can be named as a verb the operator would use out loud.
- It belongs to the view it sits in, not to a row inside it.

### Use something else when

- tabs: It only changes which panel is visible — that is Navigation (Tabs).
- chip: It carries a value the operator picked or can dismiss — that is a Chip.
- switch: It flips one setting on or off in place — that is a Switch.

### Content rules

- A verb in the imperative: "Save", "Run pipeline", "Revoke access". Never a noun like "Configuration".
- Uppercase, 12.5px, .06em tracking. One or two words; three is the ceiling and it needs a reason.
- Say what happens, not what the user wants. "Delete workspace", never "OK" or "Yes".
- No trailing punctuation, no ellipsis unless the click opens a further dialog that still needs input.
- The same action carries the same verb everywhere. "Run" is never also "Execute" or "Start".

### Examples

- [demo] Secondary
- [demo] Primary
- [demo] Ghost
- [demo] Danger
- [good] One primary, kept quiet alternative — One primary per view, with its alternative kept quiet.
- [bad] Three primaries — Never three primaries. Everything is loud, so nothing leads.
- [good] Danger names what it destroys — Danger names what it destroys, so the label survives being read alone.
- [bad] "OK" on a destructive action — Never "OK" on a destructive action — it tells the operator nothing about the consequence.
- [good] Mixed variants, one height — Mixed variants share one height, so the row keeps a single baseline.
- [bad] Resized for emphasis — Never resize a button to add emphasis — variant carries weight, size does not.

### Accessibility

- Focus ring: Every button takes a 3px --accent-soft ring with an --accent-line border on keyboard focus. Focus is never suppressed and never reduced to a colour change, so it stays visible on the filled Primary as well as on Ghost.
- Real buttons: Ghost and icon-only controls are still buttons: they take a tab stop, fire on Enter and Space, and expose a label. An icon-only button carries an aria-label matching its tooltip word for word.
- Disabled: Disabled buttons stay in the tab order as aria-disabled rather than being removed, so a keyboard operator can find the control and read why it is unavailable from the adjacent help text.
- Never colour alone: Danger is not signalled by colour alone — the label names the destruction. At 35% opacity a disabled button drops below 4.5:1, which is why disabled state is always paired with an explanatory line, never left to the eye.

### Tokens

- --accent, --bg: Primary fill and its label
- --border-2, --fg: Secondary border and label
- --panel-2: Hover fill on Secondary and Ghost
- --dim: Ghost label at rest
- --accent-soft, --accent-line: Focus ring on all variants

### Related

- chip (often-confused-with): Also clickable, but a chip carries a value the operator has chosen. A button carries an action.
- tabs (often-confused-with): Tabs switch what is shown without changing anything. If nothing is committed, it is not a button.
- modal (composes-with): Where Primary and Secondary most often appear as a pair — and where Danger is confirmed.

### Changelog

- v1.3.0 (18 Aug 2026): Focus ring unified across variants; Ghost no longer relies on a border change alone.
- v1.2.0 (15 Aug 2026): Radius locked to 2px. Active state gained the inset press shadow.
- v1.1.0 (13 Aug 2026): Danger variant added, replacing ad-hoc red text buttons.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Initial release — Primary, Secondary, Ghost across five states.

---

## Callout

Status: stable · Version: 1.0.0 · Updated: 18 Sept 2026 · /components/callout

Purpose: Reports a standing condition inside the panel or flow it belongs to.

### Description

A Callout reports a standing condition inside the panel or flow it belongs to, and stays until the operator acts on it or clears it.

It is Toast’s persistent counterpart: where a toast reports what just happened and leaves on its own in 3.2 seconds, a Callout stays exactly because the condition it names is still true. That is also the line against Modal — a Callout never blocks the rest of the page, and if the operator must answer before doing anything else, the message needed a modal, not a card.

### Anatomy

1. Icon — Names the tone at a glance, in the tone’s own colour. It is the fastest thing in the card to scan and the only place shape (not just colour) carries the tone — info, success, warning and error each get a distinct glyph.
2. Title — One short line stating the fact or outcome. It sits beside the icon, never above or below it, so the two read as a single unit before the body is reached at all.
3. Body — One to two sentences of context in --dim. This is where the detail an operator needs actually lives — the title is the headline, the body is the story.
4. Actions — Zero, one or two buttons — at most one of them primary. Optional by design: an info or success callout often has nothing to do about it and should carry none.

### Variants

- Info (--accent-2, --accent-2-line): A fact worth putting on the record — a schedule, a queue position, a setting that changed. Ice, because it refers to something rather than asking for anything.
- Success (--accent, --accent-line, --accent-soft): A completed check or a ready result — the one tone allowed the acting colour, and only because what it reports is itself an outcome, not a pending decision.
- Warning (--alarm, --alarm-line): Something worth knowing about that has not yet broken. The tone Toast intentionally has none of — a warning that must stay visible is exactly the case a self-dismissing corner message cannot serve.
- Error (--alarm, --alarm-soft): Something stopped and needs a decision. The same colour as Warning, one step darker and filled — intensity carries the escalation, not a new hue.

There is no Neutral tone here the way Toast has one — a Callout that claims no colour at all reads as unfinished, since it always sits inside a panel that already supplies neutral chrome.

### Use when

- A condition is standing, not momentary — it should still be true if the operator looks back in five minutes.
- The message belongs inside the panel or flow it is about, not floating over everything.
- Zero, one or two actions are enough to resolve or acknowledge it.

### Use something else when

- toast: The news is transient and does not need to persist — that is a Toast.
- modal: The operator must answer before doing anything else — that is a Modal.
- badge: The fact is a small, permanent label on a row — that is a Badge, not a card.

### Content rules

- Title the fact, not the feeling — "Export failed", never "Uh oh!" or "Something went wrong."
- Keep the body to one or two sentences. If it needs a third, it is a panel, not a callout.
- Name what happens if the operator does nothing, when that matters — "No action required yet" is doing real work above.
- At most one action reads as primary. A second action, if present, is always the lesser one — dismiss, view, cancel.
- Match the tone to the state, not to how urgent the writer feels — a routine reminder is Info even in a stressful week.

### Examples

- [demo] Info
- [demo] Success
- [demo] Warning
- [demo] Error
- [good] Fact-based title — Title states the fact plainly. An operator scanning the panel knows exactly what happened without reading the body.
- [bad] Feelings-first title — A feelings-first title and casual body read as unfinished copy, not a system report — name the fact, not the reaction to it.
- [good] One action — One action, unstyled as secondary since nothing here is urgent enough to demand a primary button.
- [bad] Two actions, no primary — Two actions with no clear primary compete for attention — a warning this routine should offer at most one way forward.
- [good] Error tone on a failure — Error tone on a run that stopped and needs a decision. Colour, icon and copy all agree.
- [bad] Success tone on a failure — The same failure in the Success tone — amber and a checkmark on a message that says nothing finished. Tone must match the state, not the writer’s mood.

### Accessibility

- Role by tone: Warning and Error carry role="alert" so assistive tech announces them on arrival. Info and Success carry role="status", announced politely without interrupting.
- Colour never alone: Every tone pairs its colour with a distinct icon shape and states its own severity in words — "Retry" and "no action required yet" carry the finding on their own.
- Focus order: Actions are reachable by keyboard in the order shown, primary first. A dismiss control, when present, is always last in the tab order.
- Never auto-dismissed: Unlike Toast, a Callout never times out on its own — if it should disappear by itself, it was a Toast to begin with.

### Tokens

- --accent-2: Info icon and title.
- --accent, --accent-line, --accent-soft: Success icon, title and fill — the one tone sharing the acting colour.
- --alarm, --alarm-line: Warning icon and border at reduced opacity, no fill.
- --alarm, --alarm-soft: Error icon, border and a low-opacity fill — the same hue as Warning, one step stronger.
- --dim: Body text across every tone.

### Related

- toast (often-confused-with): The transient counterpart. Reach for Toast when the message should be gone in a few seconds on its own.
- modal (contrasts-with): Where a Callout escalates once a decision must block everything else on the page.
- badge (alternative): The flat alternative. A one-word status on a row is a badge before it is ever a card.
- card (composes-with): The container a Callout usually sits inside, rather than replaces.

### Changelog

- v1.0.0 (18 Sept 2026): First specification. Named Callout to sit next to Toast without colliding, and given a Warning tone Toast deliberately omits — built from the same accent and #ff8f6b tokens Toast already established, split into two intensities rather than a new hue, to keep the amber-and-one-other-colour rule intact.

---

## Cards

Status: stable · Version: 1.2.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/card

Purpose: A bordered container that holds one whole object worth looking at on its own.

### Description

A card is a bounded surface that holds one thing worth looking at on its own.

It draws an edge around content so a page can be read as a set of objects rather than one column of text. A card stays flat in the page and stays put — the moment content needs to float over everything else it is a Modal, and when rows share the same fields and want comparing it is a Table. Only one kind of card is clickable, and that is the exception, not the default.

### Anatomy

1. Container — A 1px --border hairline on --panel, 2px radius, no shadow. Elevation belongs to overlays; a card sits flat in the page.
2. Header — 12px uppercase title at .16em on the left, optional --faint meta on the right, closed by a full-bleed hairline. Present or absent — never half-drawn.
3. Meta slot — The right end of the header carries a count, unit or status. It is reference, never an action — actions go in the body or the page header.
4. Body — 18px padding, or 14–16px when the card is a dense list. Rows inside separate with hairlines rather than gaps.

### Variants

- Plain (--border, --panel): Prose, grouped controls, anything that needs a boundary but not a name. If you find yourself adding a title later, it wanted a header all along.
- With header (--border, --panel): The default for content sections. The title names the contents so the card can be scanned in a column of siblings.
- HUD (--border, --panel, --bracket): Instrumentation only — live readouts and telemetry. The brackets are a signal that the numbers are moving, so they lose their meaning on static content.
- Stat (--fg): One number that answers one question. A label above, a value, and at most one unit of context beside it.
- Tile (--panel-2, --border-2): The only clickable card. Border and fill lift on hover, the whole surface is the hit target, and it must lead somewhere — never open a menu.

There is no elevated card. Shadow is how the system says "this floats over the page", so spending it on a card that does not float leaves nothing to say it with later.

### Use when

- The content is one whole object that makes sense read on its own.
- A page holds several such objects and the reader needs to tell where one ends.
- The grouping is stable — the same card appears in the same place tomorrow.
- It sits in the page flow, at the page's own scroll position.

### Use something else when

- modal: It must float over the page and be dismissed — that is a Modal.
- table: Every item shares the same fields and wants comparing — that is a Table.
- badge: The box would hold a single label — that is a Badge or a heading.
- empty-state: There is nothing to show yet — that is an Empty state, not a bordered void.

### Content rules

- Header titles are uppercase, 12px, .16em tracking, and name the contents rather than describing them: "Coverage", not "Here is your coverage".
- Two to four words in a title. If it needs a sentence, that sentence belongs in the body.
- The meta slot holds a count or unit and nothing else — no verbs, no punctuation, no "click to expand".
- Body copy is 13.5px --dim in full sentences. A card is not a place for orphaned fragments.
- Cards in the same grid use the same kind and the same title grammar; a mixed grid reads as an accident.

### Examples

- [demo] With header
- [demo] Plain
- [demo] HUD
- [demo] Stat
- [demo] Tile
- [good] Consistent kind and title grammar — Siblings share a kind and a title grammar, so the column scans in one pass.
- [bad] Mixed kinds in one grid — Never mix kinds in one grid — HUD brackets on static content read as an accident.
- [good] One question per stat — A stat card answers one question: label, value, one unit of context.
- [bad] A crowded stat card — Never crowd a stat card — four numbers means none of them is the answer.
- [good] One hit target, one destination — A tile is one hit target with one destination — the entire surface is clickable.
- [bad] Controls nested inside a tile — Never nest controls inside a tile — three tab stops in a clickable card fight each other.

### Accessibility

- Headings, not styling: A header title is a real heading element in the reading order, so a screen reader can jump between cards. Uppercase is a CSS transform — the accessible name stays sentence case.
- Tiles are one control: A tile is a single focusable element with one accessible name, not a div wrapping three tab stops. Enter and Space both activate it, and the focus ring wraps the whole card.
- Boundaries survive: The hairline holds 3:1 against --panel in both themes, so the card edge is still a visible boundary in high-contrast and greyscale.
- Order matters: Header precedes body in source, and a stat card announces its label before its number — "Open items, 32 of 33", never the number alone.

### Tokens

- --border, --panel: Container hairline and fill
- --border: Header divider and internal row rules
- --bracket: HUD corner marks
- --panel-2: Tile hover fill
- --dim, --faint: Body copy and meta labels

### Related

- modal (contrasts-with): A card that floats. The moment content needs a scrim and a dismiss, it stops being a card.
- table (alternative): Use instead when rows share columns. Cards are for whole objects; tables are for comparing fields.
- empty-state (composes-with): What a card body becomes when it has nothing to hold — never an empty bordered box.

### Changelog

- v1.2.0 (19 Aug 2026): Tile hover unified on --panel-2; the whole surface is now one hit target.
- v1.1.0 (15 Aug 2026): Radius locked to 2px and card shadows removed — elevation reserved for overlays.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Initial release — five kinds, header optional.

---

## Checkbox

Status: stable · Version: 1.2.0 · Updated: 20 Aug 2026 · /components/checkbox

Purpose: Records an independent yes-or-no the operator sets themselves.

### Description

A checkbox records an independent yes-or-no the operator sets themselves.

Each box stands on its own, so ticking one says nothing about the others, and nothing happens until the form is submitted. If the options are mutually exclusive it is a Radio; if the change lands the instant it is flipped it is a Switch. That deferred, independent quality is what everything below assumes.

### Anatomy

1. Box — 18px square, 1.5px border, 2px radius. Fixed at every density — the box never scales with its label.
2. Glyph — A tick when on, a dash when indeterminate, nothing when off. Drawn in --bg so it reads as cut out of the fill rather than sat on top.
3. Label — 14px --fg in sentence case, 12px from the box. It states what being checked means, not what the click does.
4. Hit row — The box and label share one 9px/11px padded row, so the whole line is clickable and clears the 32px minimum in dense chrome.

### States

- Off: The resting state. An empty box, never a greyed tick — an absent glyph is the only honest way to show "not chosen".
- On: Filled amber with a --bg tick. Amber is the act colour, and checking something is an act.
- Indeterminate: A parent whose children are partly checked. Only ever set by the system from its children — never something the operator can click into.
- Error: A required box left unchecked at submit. The border carries it, never the fill, so the state still reads at a glance.
- Disabled: Unavailable but still present, and still announced. A checkbox that vanishes reads as a bug.

There is no read-only checkbox distinct from disabled. A value the operator cannot change is either disabled, or it is not a control at all and belongs in the page as text.

### Use when

- The answer is independently yes or no, and other options do not constrain it.
- The operator may pick none, some, or all of a small set.
- The change is committed later by a submit, not the instant it is clicked.
- The full set of options is short enough to show at once — up to about seven.

### Use something else when

- radio: Exactly one option may be chosen — that is a Radio.
- switch: The setting applies immediately with no submit — that is a Switch.
- select-multi: The list is long or the chosen set must stay visible — that is Select (Multi).
- table: It selects rows to act on rather than recording a value — that belongs to Table, where selection is Ice.

### Content rules

- Label in sentence case, 14px, no terminal punctuation: "Send weekly digest", never "SEND WEEKLY DIGEST" or "Send weekly digest."
- Phrase the label as the positive statement being agreed to, so checking always means yes. "Include archived", never "Do not include archived".
- Say what the state means, not what the click does — "Retry failed steps", never "Click to retry".
- Keep labels to a line where possible; if the rule needs explaining, put a 12.5px --mute line beneath rather than lengthening the label.
- A group of checkboxes shares one grammar and one subject, so the set can be read as a list rather than five unrelated sentences.

### Examples

- [demo] Retry failed steps
- [good] Labels state the positive — Labels state the positive, so a tick always means yes.
- [bad] A negated "don't include" label — Never negate a label — a ticked "don't include" forces the reader to do logic.
- [good] Detail beneath a one-line label — Detail goes on a --mute line beneath, keeping the label to one line.
- [bad] A label grown into a sentence — Never grow the label into a sentence — the box stops being scannable.
- [good] Indeterminate derived from children — Indeterminate is derived from children — the system sets it, never a click.
- [bad] Indeterminate as a third answer — Never use indeterminate as a third answer an operator can choose.

### Accessibility

- Real inputs: Every checkbox is a real input with a bound label, so it takes a tab stop, toggles on Space, and announces its checked state. Indeterminate is set through the DOM property, which is what lets a screen reader say "partially checked".
- The row is the target: The 18px box is smaller than any hit-target floor, so the padded row carries the interaction. Clicking the label toggles the box — a label that does nothing is a broken control.
- Never colour alone: Checked is signalled by the tick as well as the fill, and error by a border plus a message. Under greyscale the tick still reads, which is the test.
- Groups announce: A set of related checkboxes shares a group label so its purpose is announced once, and the reading order follows the visual order down the column.

### Tokens

- --border-2: Box border when off
- --accent, --bg: Fill when on, and the glyph cut out of it
- --accent-soft, --accent-line: Focus ring and its border
- --alarm-line: Error border
- --fg: Label, and the box border on hover

### Related

- radio (alternative): Use instead when the options are mutually exclusive. A checkbox answers one yes-or-no; a radio picks one of several.
- switch (alternative): Use instead when the change takes effect immediately. Checkboxes wait for a submit; switches do not.
- select-multi (alternative): Use instead past roughly seven options, or when the chosen set needs to stay visible after the list closes.

### Changelog

- v1.2.0 (20 Aug 2026): Indeterminate documented as system-set only; hover tint unified with Radio.
- v1.1.0 (15 Aug 2026): Box radius locked to 2px; focus moved to the soft ring.
- v1.0.0 (12 Aug 2026): Initial release — real inputs, eight-state matrix.

## Chips

Status: stable · Version: 1.2.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/chip

Purpose: A round-ended token representing a value the operator chose, such as a filter. The operator can dismiss it.

### Description

A chip is a small pressable pill carrying a value the operator has chosen.

It is theirs, not the system's: they turn it on, combine it with others, or take it away. That ownership is the whole distinction from a Badge, which is the same size and casing but assigned by the system and inert. A chip also never commits anything — it narrows what is shown, so if the press has a consequence it is a Button.

### Anatomy

1. Container — A 20px pill — the one deliberate exception to the sharp-radius lock. The round shape is what tells an operator this is theirs to press, not the system's to assign.
2. Label — 11.5px at .1em, uppercase. It names the value the chip carries, never the act of pressing it.
3. Padding — 5px vertical, 13px horizontal, widening to 9px on the right when a dismiss glyph is present so the label never crowds it.
4. Dismiss — An optional × on removable chips only. It is a second hit target inside the chip, so it appears only where removal is the point.

### Variants

- Filter (--border, --dim): The default. One of a small set, at most one active at a time, narrowing what is already on screen. Pressing it changes the view, never the data.
- Toggle (--border, --dim): Same shape, but several can be on at once. Use when the facets combine rather than replace each other.
- Removable (--border, --dim, --mute): Carries a value the operator has already committed — a token in Select (Multi), an applied filter. The × is the only way out.
- Active (--accent, --accent-soft): Not a variant so much as the on state: amber border, soft amber fill, amber label. Only ever one visual treatment for on.

There is no tonal chip — no info chip, no danger chip. Amber means on and that is the only colour a chip carries, because a coloured pill the operator can press would compete with the one action the page is actually asking for.

### Use when

- The operator is narrowing a view they can already see.
- The facets are few enough to show at once, and worth showing without a click.
- The choice is theirs to make and theirs to undo, with no submit in between.
- A committed value needs to stay visible so it can be taken away later.

### Use something else when

- badge: The system assigns it and it cannot be pressed — that is a Badge.
- button: Pressing it commits or changes something — that is a Button.
- tabs: It switches between whole views — that is Navigation (Tabs).
- select-multi: The options outgrow a single row — that is Select (Multi).

### Content rules

- Uppercase, 11.5px, .1em tracking — the same casing as a badge, so the shape rather than the type carries the difference.
- One or two words naming the value: "OPEN", "LAST 7 DAYS". Never a verb — "FILTER" tells the operator nothing about what they get.
- Keep a row of chips parallel in grammar and length; a set that mixes "OPEN" with "AWAITING MANUAL REVIEW" reads as unfinished.
- No counts inside the label. If the number matters, it belongs in the results heading, not baked into the chip.
- The same facet uses the same word wherever it appears, so a chip learned in one workspace is recognised in the next.

### Examples

- [demo] Filter
- [demo] Toggle
- [demo] Removable
- [demo] Active
- [good] One treatment for on — One visual treatment for on, and the labels name values in parallel grammar.
- [bad] Tonal chips — Never give chips tonal colours — amber means on, and nothing else competes for it.
- [good] A short row shown in full — A short row shown in full, so every facet is visible without a click.
- [bad] Chips wrapped onto three lines — Never wrap chips onto three lines — past about seven this wanted a Select (Multi).
- [good] Removable chips as tokens — Removable chips carry committed values, each with its own dismiss target.
- [bad] An action inside a chip — Never put an action in a chip — a verb in a pill is a button wearing the wrong shape.

### Accessibility

- Pressed, not checked: A filter or toggle chip is a button that reports aria-pressed, so a screen reader announces "Open, pressed" rather than leaving the operator to infer state from colour.
- Two targets, two labels: On a removable chip the body and the × are separate controls. The × carries its own label naming what it removes — "Remove Open" — never a bare "close".
- Never colour alone: On state is amber border plus amber fill plus amber label plus aria-pressed. Three visual signals and one semantic one, because a single hue shift is invisible to a third of operators.
- Hit area: The pill is 5px/13px padded to clear 32px in dense chrome. The × gets its own padding rather than shrinking the label's target.

### Tokens

- --border, --dim: Resting border and label
- --border-2, --fg: Hover border and label
- --accent, --accent-soft: Active border, fill and label
- --accent-soft, --accent-line: Focus ring and its border
- --mute: Dismiss glyph, brightening to --fg on hover

### Related

- badge (contrasts-with): Same size, opposite ownership. A badge is system-assigned and inert; if it can be pressed it belongs here.
- select-multi (alternative): Where removable chips live as tokens. Use it instead when the option list is long enough to need a menu.
- tabs (contrasts-with): Tabs switch between whole views; chips narrow the one view you are already in.

### Changelog

- v1.2.0 (21 Aug 2026): Removable variant documented; dismiss glyph given its own hit area and label.
- v1.1.0 (16 Aug 2026): Pill radius kept at 20px as a named exception to the sharp-radius lock.
- v1.0.0 (12 Aug 2026): Initial release — filter and toggle, single active treatment.

---

## Drawer

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 23 Aug 2026 · /components/drawer

Purpose: A side panel showing the details of one thing without leaving the current view.

### Description

A drawer is a full-height panel that slides in from the right and sits beside the work instead of on top of it.

It is the surface for detail, settings and editing — anything where the page behind stays relevant and the operator should still be able to read it. That is the line against a Modal: a modal interrupts and demands one answer before anything else happens, while a drawer accompanies. If the operator can safely keep looking at the table they came from, it is a drawer.

### Anatomy

1. Scrim — A dim over the work behind, never a blur strong enough to hide it. It is there to say the panel has focus, not to take the page away — a click on it closes the drawer.
2. Panel and left hairline — Full height, anchored to the right, square on every corner. The 1px left hairline is the only thing separating it from the page, which is why it is the one border allowed to carry accent.
3. Header — The record's name at 17.5px with a tracked meta line under it, and the close glyph in the far corner. It stays pinned so the operator always knows what they are looking at.
4. Body — The only scrolling region. One column at SM and MD; labels sit above values so a long value can wrap without breaking the grid.
5. Footer — Pinned to the bottom, actions right-aligned, primary last. It holds the single commit for everything in the body — nothing above it saves on its own.

### Variants

- SM (--bg, --border, --accent): 360px wide. One column, labels above values, no nested panels.
- MD (--bg, --border, --accent): 480px wide, full height, 1px left hairline, no radius on the outer edge. Slides in over 260ms; the scrim dims rather than blurs the work behind it.
- LG (--bg, --border, --accent): 720px wide. Two columns are allowed at this size only; keep the primary action pinned to the footer so it survives long scrolls.

There is no full-screen drawer. A panel that covers the page has stopped accompanying the work and become a route of its own — at that point it is a page, and it should have a URL, a breadcrumb and a back button rather than a scrim.

### Use when

- The operator is inspecting or editing one record while the list it came from stays useful.
- The content is longer than a modal should be — a form with sections, an activity log, a config.
- They will move through several records in turn, and reopening a centred dialog each time would be punishing.
- The work behind must remain readable for reference while the panel is open.

### Use something else when

- modal: One decision must be made before anything else can proceed — that is a Modal.
- popover: It is a short set of choices anchored to the control that opened it — that is a Popover.
- toast: It is only confirming that something happened — that is a Toast.

### Content rules

- The header names the thing, not the task: "Details", "AUT·02" — never "Edit item details" repeated from the button that opened it.
- The meta line under the title carries the identifier and nothing else, so the operator can quote it without opening anything further.
- Labels are sentence case and sit above their values; a value that is empty says so in --faint rather than leaving a blank.
- The footer verb states the outcome — "Save changes", "Run now" — and its neighbour is always the plain word "Cancel".
- If the body needs more than two headed sections, the content has outgrown a drawer and belongs on a page.

### Examples

- [demo] Demo
- [demo] SM
- [demo] MD
- [demo] LG
- [good] Pinned footer commit — The commit lives in a pinned footer, so it survives any length of scroll.
- [bad] Commits scattered in the body — Never scatter commits through the body — the operator stops knowing what is saved.
- [good] One panel — One panel, and the work behind it still legible through a dimming scrim.
- [bad] A drawer on a drawer — Never stack a drawer on a drawer — the second one has no way back that reads as one.
- [good] Named header, visible close — A header that names the record, with the close glyph in its own corner.
- [bad] No title, no visible close — Never open a drawer with no title and no visible close — the scrim is not an exit.

### Accessibility

- Dialog, and modal about it: The panel is role="dialog" with aria-modal, labelled by its own header, so the announcement names the record rather than "dialog".
- Focus in, focus back: Focus moves to the panel on open and is trapped inside it; on close it returns to the exact control that opened the drawer, never to the top of the page.
- Two ways out: Escape and the close glyph both dismiss, and the scrim click is a third — but the glyph is the only one a keyboard user is required to find, so it is never hidden on hover.
- Reading order: Header, then body, then footer in the DOM, matching what the eye does. The pinned footer is last in source even though it is visually fixed.

### Tokens

- --bg: Panel surface.
- --border-2: Left hairline against the page.
- --border: Header and footer rules.
- --accent: Primary commit in the footer.
- --dim, --mute: Body copy and meta line.

### Related

- modal (often-confused-with): A modal interrupts and needs one answer; a drawer accompanies work that carries on around it.
- popover (often-confused-with): A popover is anchored to its trigger and holds a few choices; a drawer is anchored to the viewport and holds a record.
- table (often-confused-with): The table is where drawers are opened from, and the row stays highlighted while its panel is up.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (23 Aug 2026): Scrim changed from blur to dim so the work behind stays readable; footer commit made mandatory.
- v1.0.1 (19 Aug 2026): LG widened to 720px and allowed two columns; full-screen drawer ruled out.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Drawer introduced at three widths with a pinned header and footer.

---

## Empty state

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/empty-state

Purpose: What a region says when it has loaded successfully and has nothing to show.

### Description

An empty state is what a region says when it has loaded successfully and has nothing to show.

It is a statement of fact with a way forward, not an apology and not decoration. The line against Loading is certainty: loading means the answer is unknown, empty means the answer is known and it is none. Showing an empty state while a request is still in flight is the one failure mode that matters here, because it tells the operator to act on a conclusion the system has not reached.

### Anatomy

1. Region — The empty state borrows the frame it sits in and adds none of its own. No dashed box, no nested card — the panel or table already drew the boundary.
2. Mark — One 22px hairline glyph in --faint, naming the kind of thing that is missing. It is the only ornament allowed, and it never carries accent — nothing here is live.
3. Headline — 14.5px in --dim, stating the fact in the operator’s vocabulary: "No runs in this window". Not a greeting, not an apology.
4. Support line — 12.5px in --faint, capped near 330px so it stays one or two lines. It says what would appear here and how it gets here — the only teaching this component does.
5. Action — At most one, and only when there is genuinely a next step. Primary for a first run, ghost for undoing a filter, absent when the operator cannot act.

### Variants

- First run (--faint, --dim, --accent): Nothing exists yet because nothing has been made. This is the only kind that earns a primary button, because creating the first record is genuinely the next thing to do.
- No results (--faint, --dim, --border-2): Records exist, but the operator’s own query excluded them. Name the filter that did it and offer to undo it — the way out is backwards, not forwards, so the action is a ghost.
- Restricted (--faint, --dim): There is content, but not for this operator. Say so plainly and name who can change it. Offering a button they cannot use is worse than offering none.

There is no error variant and no illustrated variant. A failed request is not empty — it gets an inline error with a retry, because "nothing here" would quietly turn a broken system into a normal one. And art in place of data reads as celebration; a 22px hairline glyph is as much decoration as this system allows.

### Use when

- The request finished and the result is legitimately nothing.
- A region would otherwise be a blank rectangle with no explanation.
- There is a clear next step, or a clear reason there is none.
- The operator’s own filter is why they see nothing, and they may not remember setting it.

### Use something else when

- loading: The answer is not known yet — that is Loading.
- toast: Something was completed and needs acknowledging — that is a Toast.

### Content rules

- The headline states what is absent, not how the system feels: "No runs in this window", never "Oops, nothing here!".
- Never apologise and never thank — an empty list is an ordinary condition, and treating it as a failure teaches operators to distrust it.
- The support line answers one question: what would be here, and what puts it here. Anything more belongs in documentation.
- When a filter is the cause, name the filter in the headline and say how many records it hid, so the operator can judge whether to clear it.
- One action at most, verb-first and specific — "Schedule a run", never "Get started" — and no action at all rather than a disabled one.

### Examples

- [demo] First run
- [demo] No results
- [demo] Restricted
- [good] The fact, one line, one way forward — The fact, one line of use, and exactly one way forward.
- [bad] An apology instead of a fact — Never apologise — the API allows only one action, so a second primary is a mistake this component can't make, but tone still can.
- [good] The filter stays named and undoable — The filter stays visible, is named in the line, and can be undone from here.
- [bad] A dashed box around the state — Never wrap an empty state in its own box, and never say "No data" without saying why — the region it sits in already drew the boundary.
- [good] Naming who has access — When there is no next step, name who has it instead of inventing a button.

### Accessibility

- Not an alert: The region is a plain labelled container, not role="alert". An empty result is not urgent, and announcing it as an alert interrupts whatever the operator was reading.
- Announced once: When the state replaces loaded content — after a filter change — the region is aria-live="polite" so the headline is read once, and the count in the support line is part of that sentence rather than a separate node.
- Decorative mark: The glyph is aria-hidden. It repeats what the headline already says, so a screen reader hearing it twice would only add noise.
- Measured contrast: --dim on --panel-2 clears 7:1 and the --faint support line clears 4.6:1 at 12.5px. Faint is the quietest token allowed to carry a sentence — below it, text becomes decoration.

### Tokens

- --faint: Mark
- --mute: Support line
- --dim: Headline
- --panel-2: Surface, inherited from the region
- --accent: Primary action — first run only
- --border-2: Ghost action border

### Related

- loading (contrasts-with): Loading means the answer is unknown; empty means it is known and it is none. Never show this one while a request is in flight.
- table (composes-with): A table’s empty state replaces the rows and keeps the header, so the columns still explain what would have been listed.
- card (composes-with): A card body with nothing in it becomes this — the card keeps its frame and the empty state fills the inside.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (23 Aug 2026): Three kinds separated — first run, no results, restricted — with the primary action limited to first run. Error variant ruled out.
- v1.0.1 (17 Aug 2026): Illustration removed in favour of a single 22px hairline mark in --faint.
- v1.0.0 (9 Aug 2026): Empty state introduced with mark, headline, support line and optional action.

---

## Header

Status: stable · Version: 1.0.0 · Updated: 5 Oct 2026 · /components/header

Purpose: Names the selected top-level module and carries ambient reference and the operator's own identity. Chrome, not content.

### Description

The header is the 52px bar pinned to the top of every screen, naming the selected module and carrying ambient reference and the operator's own identity.

It is chrome, not content: it says where you are in the product and who you are signed in as, and nothing about the page underneath. That is the line against the page header inside the content column — breadcrumb, title, status, actions all live there, because they change with the route. Anything that would need to change when the operator navigates does not belong in this bar.

### Anatomy

1. Bar — 52px tall, pinned to the top, with a blurred 60% background so content stays visible passing under it. Its only hard edge is the 1px bottom hairline, and its left edge starts where the main nav ends.
2. Module title — The selected top-level rail item, named at the left edge in --accent: its glyph, its name, and a SYS code. It moves with the rail, never with the route.
3. Ambient cluster — Date in --dim, clock in --mute, split by a 1px 12px divider. Read-only by design — there is nothing here to click and nothing here to act on.
4. Identity square — A 34px square opening the operator menu: appearance, preferences, sign out. Square rather than round, because a circular avatar would read as a chip.
5. Status dot — An 8px amber dot ringed in --bg, pulsing on a 2.6s cycle. It is the single live element in the bar, which is exactly why it is legible — one moving thing in otherwise still chrome.

### Variants

- Module title (--accent): The selected top-level rail item — its own glyph, name and a SYS code — anchoring the left edge that the brand lockup vacated. It only ever names the top level; it never follows the operator into a sub-page.
- Ambient (--dim, --mute): Date then clock, split by a 1px 12px divider. Reference only — nothing in this zone is clickable, and nothing in it is ever amber, because a workspace where the wall clock competes with an alert is a workspace nobody reads.
- Identity (--accent, --fg): A square opening the operator menu — appearance, preferences, sign out. The status dot is the single live element in the whole bar, which is what makes it readable at a glance.

There is no search field, no notification tray and no page action in this bar, and no compact variant of it. Global search belongs to the command palette on a keystroke; alerts belong to the surface that owns them; a page's primary action belongs beside that page's title. Nothing here changes with the route below it — not even the module title, which tracks the rail, not the page.

### States

- Default: Translucent bar, --dim date, --mute clock, --fg identity square.
- Live: The status dot pulses on a 2.6s cycle — the one moving element in the bar.
- Menu open: The identity square's operator menu is open, anchored below it.
- Focus: 2px accent ring on the identity square.

### Use when

- Ambient reference the operator glances at rather than acts on.
- Who is signed in, and the menu that changes that.
- State that is true on every screen, at every route, without exception.

### Use something else when

- main-rail: Moving between workspaces — that is Navigation (Main).
- subnav: Moving within one — that is Navigation (Subnav).
- toast: Anything that has just happened — that is a Toast.

### Content rules

- The bar carries no brand mark — the lockup lives in the main rail now. Its left edge instead names the selected top-level module, so the header always says where the rail has you.
- The date reads WED 23 AUG 2026: uppercase, weekday first, no punctuation, so its width barely changes across the year.
- The clock is 24-hour with seconds. Seconds are what make it read as a live instrument rather than a decoration nobody trusts.
- No page title, breadcrumb or record name ever appears in the bar — if it changes with the route, it belongs to the page header below.
- The identity square carries no count, no initials and no label; the status dot is the only thing it is allowed to say.

### Examples

- [demo] Header
- [good] Chrome only — Three zones, one accent, and the bar reads in half a second.
- [bad] A fourth zone — Never grow a fourth zone — search, counts and page actions each have a home already.
- [good] Ambient stays grey — Ambient stays grey: date in --dim, clock in --mute, divided by a hairline.
- [bad] Accent clock — Never let the clock take accent — amber in the chrome must mean something happened.

### Accessibility

- Banner, not nav: The bar is the page's banner landmark and contains no navigation list. The main rail is the nav landmark, so a screen-reader user jumping between landmarks does not meet the same links twice.
- Named identity control: The identity square is a button whose accessible name carries both the operator and the state — "Aria, active" — because the dot alone is invisible to anyone not looking at it.
- Quiet clock: The ambient cluster is not a live region. A clock announcing itself every second would make the rest of the screen unusable, so it is read only when the operator moves to it.
- Measured contrast: --fg wordmark clears 12:1 over the translucent bar, --dim date 7.1:1, --mute clock 4.8:1 at 12px. Contrast is measured against the darkest content that can scroll beneath, not against --bg.

### Tokens

- --border-2: Bottom hairline and identity square
- --accent: Module title icon, label and code; operator status dot
- --dim: Date, module code
- --mute: Clock

### Related

- main-rail (composes-with): The rail owns the product mark and moving between workspaces; the header names which top-level item is selected. They share one edge and never share a control.
- subnav (contrasts-with): Subnav sits inside the content column and changes with the route — which is precisely what the header may never do.
- popover (composes-with): The operator menu is a popover anchored to the identity square, so the bar itself never grows to hold it.

### Changelog

- v1.0.0 (5 Oct 2026): Header ported: translucent 52px bar, module title, ambient cluster, identity square with an Appearance (theme) control in its operator menu.
