## Loading

Status: stable · Version: 1.2.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/loading

Purpose: What a region shows while it still does not know the answer.

### Description

Loading is what a region shows while it still does not know the answer.

It is the only place in the system where amber moves without something having happened, and it earns that because motion is the one honest way to say “still working”. The line against Progress is knowledge: progress states a measured fraction of a known total, loading states nothing but that work is under way. Never fake one as the other — a bar creeping to 90% and stopping is worse than a sweep that admits it cannot say.

### Anatomy

1. Region — The waiting area, scoped as tightly as possible — one panel, one row, one field. It keeps the frame it already had, so the page does not reflow when the answer arrives.
2. Track — A 2px hairline in --accent-line, one per line of text that has not arrived. Widths are deliberately unequal — 86%, 64%, 74% — because prose does not arrive in a rectangle.
3. Sweep — A gradient a third of the track wide, travelling left to right over 1.8s and staggered 220ms per track. The direction is the direction of reading, which is what makes it feel like text being written.
4. Phase label — 11.5px in --faint, mono, prefixed // and uppercased: the one piece of real information in the whole component. It names what the system is doing right now, not that it is busy.
5. Caret — A 5×11px amber block blinking on a 1s step, sitting where the next character would land. It is the smallest unit of liveness the system has, and the only one allowed inside a table row.

### Variants

- Sweep stack (--accent-line, --accent): The default, and the house style. Two or three hairlines of unequal width, staggered by 220ms, standing in for text that has not arrived. Use it when an agent is working and the shape of the answer is not yet known.
- Skeleton (--border, --border-2): For layouts whose shape is already known — table rows, a card grid. It holds the exact geometry the content will occupy so nothing jumps when it lands, and it is grey, not amber: the shape is the message, not the motion.
- Inline caret (--accent, --mute): For dense chrome where a stack will not fit: a table row mid-refresh, a button mid-submit, a status line. The phase name carries the meaning and the caret carries the liveness.

There is no spinner in this system, and no full-screen loading overlay. A rotating disc says only that something is happening somewhere, which the operator already assumed; and blanking the whole workspace to say it takes away the very context they were reading. Loading is always scoped to the region that is actually waiting.

### Use when

- The wait will exceed about 400ms — below that, showing anything only flickers.
- The duration cannot be measured, so no honest percentage exists.
- A named phase can be reported, and it will change as the work moves on.
- The region that is waiting can be pointed at precisely.

### Use something else when

- progress: The total is known and the fraction is real — that is Progress.
- empty-state: The work finished with nothing to show — that is an Empty state.
- toast: The work finished elsewhere and needs acknowledging — that is a Toast.

### Content rules

- The phase label is a present participle in mono uppercase behind a // prefix: "// ANALYZING", "// READING 214 RUNS".
- Name the phase, never the state: "// SYNCING" tells the operator something; "// LOADING" and "Please wait" tell them nothing they had not worked out.
- Include a real count when one exists — it turns an indefinite wait into a measurable one without pretending to know the total time.
- Change the label as the work moves through phases. A label that never changes for thirty seconds reads as a hang.
- Past about ten seconds, say what is slow — "// WAITING ON UPSTREAM" — rather than leaving the same phase spinning.

### Examples

- [demo] Sweep stack
- [demo] Skeleton
- [demo] Inline caret
- [good] A named phase with a real count — A named phase with a real count — the wait reports what it is doing.
- [bad] A spinner and “Loading…” — Never a spinner, and never "Loading…" — neither says anything the operator did not know.
- [good] A skeleton in the exact geometry of the rows — A skeleton in the exact geometry of the rows, so nothing moves when data lands.
- [bad] Generic grey slabs — Never generic grey slabs — a skeleton that lies about the layout causes the jump it was meant to prevent.
- [good] One row refreshing in place — One row refreshing keeps its data and reports in place with a caret.
- [bad] Replacing data with skeletons on refresh — Never replace data already on screen with skeletons on refresh — the operator loses what they were reading.

### Accessibility

- Busy, announced once: The region carries aria-busy while it waits and its label is announced politely a single time. The sweep itself is aria-hidden — an animation has nothing to say out loud.
- Phase changes are polite: When the phase name changes the new one is announced, at most every few seconds. A label that updates per frame would make a screen reader unusable.
- Reduced motion: Under prefers-reduced-motion the sweep stops travelling and the tracks hold a static amber segment; the caret stops blinking and stays lit. The information survives without the movement.
- Skeletons are silent: Skeleton bars are aria-hidden and carry no text. They exist to hold geometry, and announcing "loading" once per row would say the same thing twelve times.

### Tokens

- --accent-line: Track behind the sweep
- --accent: Sweep gradient and caret
- --border, --border-2: Skeleton bars
- --mute: Phase label

### Related

- progress (contrasts-with): Progress reports a measured fraction of a known total. The moment you can honestly say 40%, stop using this.
- empty-state (contrasts-with): What replaces this when the work finishes with nothing to show. Never show both, and never show empty while this is still running.
- table (composes-with): Tables load as skeleton rows and refresh in place with a row caret — the two variants that are not the sweep stack.

### Changelog

- v1.2.0 (23 Aug 2026): Three variants separated by what is known; spinner and full-screen overlay ruled out for good.
- v1.1.0 (15 Aug 2026): Phase label made mandatory alongside the sweep stack; reduced-motion fallback specified.
- v1.0.0 (7 Aug 2026): Sweep stack introduced at 1.8s with a 220ms stagger.

## Navigation (Main)

Status: stable · Version: 1.0.0 · Updated: 5 Oct 2026 · /components/main-rail

Purpose: The full-height column on the left that moves the operator between workspaces. The one navigation in the product that never changes.

### Description

The main rail is the full-height column on the left that moves the operator between workspaces.

It is the only navigation in the product that never changes: the same items, in the same order, on every screen. That fixity is the point — it is hit fifty times a day and must be answerable by muscle memory rather than by reading. The line against Navigation (Subnav) is scope: the rail chooses which workspace you are in, the subnav chooses where you are inside it. One level each, and neither borrows the other's job.

### Anatomy

1. Rail — A full-height column on --bg with a single hairline against the content. It scrolls only if the workspace list outgrows the viewport, and it never scrolls the launcher or System out of reach.
2. Active indicator — A 2px amber rail pinned to the left edge of the current row, 16px tall. It is the one piece of the nav that says where you are, so nothing else in the rail is allowed to use it.
3. Row — 40px tall with 9px padding — comfortable enough to hit without looking. Hover fills with --panel-2 and takes no rail, which is what keeps hover and active distinguishable.
4. Icon — A 22px glyph in a fixed 22px box, so icons stay in a straight column whether labels are shown or not. Collapsing the rail changes nothing about their position.
5. Collapse row — Set apart by 14px at the foot of the rail, in --dim so it reads as chrome rather than a destination. It is the only row that does not navigate.
6. Brand lockup — The mark and wordmark, pinned above the rows behind a hairline. It is the way back to the launcher and, since the header dropped it, the only place the wordmark appears at all.

### Variants

- Expanded (--accent, --fg, --panel-2): The default, and what a new operator sees. Labels are what make the rail learnable, so it starts open and stays open unless the operator chooses otherwise.
- Collapsed (--accent, --fg, --panel-2): For operators who know the rail by shape and want the width back for their work. Every item stays present and in the same order — only the labels leave, into a native tooltip. The content shifts by exactly the difference over 260ms.

There is no flyout, no nested tree and no "more" overflow. A rail that hides items behind a second interaction is no longer answerable by memory, and a second level of nesting is what the subnav is for.

### States

- Default: --fg label, no fill.
- Hover: --panel-2 fill, no rail.
- Active: Amber rail and label.
- Focus: 2px accent ring.

### Use when

- A workspace the operator returns to on their own, not one they are sent to.
- A destination with its own subnav and its own sense of "home".
- Something that survives a redesign of the page it opens.
- The launcher, and the system — the two fixed ends of the list.

### Use something else when

- subnav: A page inside a workspace — that is Navigation (Subnav).
- tabs: A view of the same page — that is Navigation (Tabs).
- button: Anything that performs an action — that is a Button.

### Content rules

- One word per row wherever possible — "Fleet", "Research", "Console". Two only when one would be ambiguous.
- Labels are nouns, never verbs: the rail names places, and a verb in a place list reads as an action that will fire.
- Sentence case at 12px with .08em tracking. The rail is the one navigation that is not uppercased, so it stays quieter than the chrome around it.
- The label in the rail matches the page title it opens, word for word. A rename in one place is a rename in both.
- Collapsed rows keep their label in a Tooltip on hover — the text is never dropped, only moved.

### Examples

- [demo] Navigation (Main)
- [good] Hover fills, active takes the rail — Hover fills; only active takes the amber rail and label. The two never look alike.
- [bad] Hover given the active treatment — Never give hover the active treatment — the operator loses track of where they are.
- [good] Collapsed keeps every item — Collapsed keeps every item, in the same order, at the same height.
- [bad] Items folded into overflow — Never fold items into an overflow menu — a hidden rail cannot be learned.

### Accessibility

- Nav landmark: The rail is the page's single nav landmark, holding one list of links. The header is the banner, so landmark navigation never presents the same destinations twice.
- Current page: The active row carries aria-current="page", which is what announces position. The amber rail is the visual echo of that attribute, never the only signal.
- Collapsed still labelled: In the 56px rail each link keeps its accessible name; only the visible text is replaced by a Tooltip. Nothing becomes an unlabelled icon.
- Focus and hit size: Rows are 40px tall with a visible focus ring drawn inside the rail, so keyboard focus is never clipped by the hairline edge.

### Tokens

- --fg: Resting labels and icons
- --panel-2: Row hover fill
- --accent: Active rail and label
- --dim: Collapse row

### Related

- subnav (contrasts-with): The subnav moves within a workspace and changes per route — the level of nesting this rail refuses to carry.
- header (composes-with): The header starts where this rail ends. It used to share the brand lockup too; now the rail carries the mark alone and the header opens empty on the left.
- tabs (contrasts-with): Tabs switch views of one page. If the destination has its own subnav, it was a rail item instead.

### Changelog

- v1.0.0 (5 Oct 2026): Navigation (Main) ported: two-width rail (216px expanded, 56px collapsed), amber active indicator, collapsed-row tooltips, keyboard-complete collapse toggle.
- v0.1.0 (2 Oct 2026): Draft stub created so Scrollbar's own relationship had somewhere real to point.

---

## Modal

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 24 Aug 2026 · /components/modal

Purpose: An overlay that must be answered before the operator can do anything else.

### Description

A modal is a centred dialog that stops the workspace until the operator answers it.

It is the most expensive surface in the system, because it takes away every other choice on the screen. That cost is the whole reason it exists: a decision that must not be missed. The line against a Drawer is whether the work behind may continue — a drawer accompanies, a modal interrupts. If the operator could reasonably ignore it for a minute and carry on, it was never a modal.

### Anatomy

1. Scrim — A dim over the whole workspace, blurred enough to say the page is out of reach but not enough to hide it. Clicking it closes a non-destructive modal and does nothing on a destructive one.
2. Dialog — Centred, square-cornered, on --panel-2 with a --border-2 hairline and a soft drop shadow — one of the few surfaces in the system allowed elevation, because it genuinely floats.
3. Header — The question itself, set as a question: "Delete 'rebalance'?". The close glyph sits opposite it and is always present except on a destructive confirm.
4. Body — One or two sentences naming the consequence, in the operator's vocabulary. It never scrolls: if it would, the content was too big for a modal.
5. Footer — Exactly two actions, right-aligned, primary last. The primary repeats the verb from the header so the operator can read the header and the button and nothing in between.

### Variants

- SM (--panel-2, --border-2, --accent): One question, two buttons, no scrolling. Use SM for destructive confirms and nothing else.
- MD (--panel-2, --border-2, --accent): The default. Fits a short form — up to six fields — or a decision that needs a paragraph of context. If it starts to scroll, it belongs in a drawer.
- LG (--panel-2, --border-2, --accent): For dense content that must stay modal: side-by-side comparisons, a table of affected records, a diff. Body scrolls internally; header and footer stay pinned. Past this size, use a full page.

There is no XL modal and no full-screen modal. Past LG the dialog stops being a decision and becomes a workspace, and a workspace that cannot be left is a trap — that content belongs in a Drawer or on a page of its own.

### Use when

- The action is destructive or irreversible and deserves a deliberate pause.
- Nothing else on the screen makes sense until this is answered.
- The whole decision fits on one screen with no internal scrolling.
- There are exactly two ways out, and both are named.

### Use something else when

- drawer: The work behind stays relevant — that is a Drawer.
- popover: It is a few choices anchored to the control that opened it — that is a Popover.
- toast: It only reports that something happened — that is a Toast.
- drawer: It is a form with sections, or anything that scrolls — that is a drawer or a page.

### Content rules

- The header is the question, not the feature: "Delete 'rebalance'?" — never "Confirm deletion" and never "Are you sure?".
- Name the object in quotes and the consequence in the body: what stops, what survives, and whether it can be undone.
- The primary button repeats the verb — "Delete workflow", "Stop runs" — so the action is legible without reading back up.
- The secondary is always the plain word "Cancel". It is not a variation and it is never styled to compete.
- Two actions maximum. A third option means the decision has not been framed yet, not that the footer needs another button.

### Examples

- [demo] Demo
- [demo] SM
- [demo] MD
- [demo] LG
- [good] Named object, repeated verb — The object is named, the consequence stated, and the button repeats the verb.
- [bad] "Are you sure?" with OK — Never "Are you sure?" with OK — the operator has to guess what OK agrees to.
- [good] Two ways out — Two ways out, one of them primary, and no third path competing.
- [bad] Four actions in a footer — Never four actions in a footer — a modal with a menu in it is a decision nobody can make.
- [good] One field — One field is fine — a single input is still one decision.
- [bad] A scrolling form — Never a scrolling form in a modal — if it needs sections, it needed a drawer.

### Accessibility

- Dialog and modal: role="dialog" with aria-modal, labelled by the header and described by the body, so the announcement carries the question and the consequence together.
- Focus is trapped: Focus moves to the dialog on open and cycles inside it — this is the one place a trap is correct. On close it returns to the control that opened the modal.
- Escape, always: Escape closes any modal, including destructive ones, because cancelling is never the dangerous path. The scrim click is only wired up when nothing can be lost.
- No default on destruct: The primary is focused on a benign modal so Enter confirms; on a destructive one focus lands on Cancel, so a stray keystroke cannot delete anything.

### Tokens

- --panel-2: Dialog surface.
- --border-2: Dialog hairline.
- --border: Header and footer rules.
- --accent: Primary action.
- --dim, --mute: Body copy and Cancel.

### Related

- drawer (often-confused-with): A drawer accompanies work that carries on; a modal stops it. Anything that scrolls belongs to the drawer.
- popover (often-confused-with): A popover is anchored to its trigger and dismissible by looking away; a modal is centred and must be answered.
- toast (often-confused-with): A toast reports what already happened. If no answer is needed, the modal was the wrong shape.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (23 Aug 2026): Footer capped at two actions; destructive modals now focus Cancel and ignore scrim clicks.
- v1.0.2 (18 Aug 2026): Internal scrolling ruled out; oversized content redirected to the drawer.
- v1.0.0 (10 Aug 2026): Modal introduced at three widths with scrim, header, body and footer.

---

## Popover

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 24 Aug 2026 · /components/popover

Purpose: A small anchored overlay holding a short action list or a few detail pairs.

### Description

A popover is a small surface anchored to the control that opened it, holding actions or detail that would otherwise clutter the page.

It is opened by a click, dismissed by looking away, and it never blocks the page behind it. That is the line against Modal: a modal is centred, scrimmed and must be answered before work continues, while a popover is peripheral and costs nothing to abandon. Against Tooltip the line is the click — anything that opens on hover is a tooltip and may contain nothing the operator has to reach.

### Anatomy

1. Trigger — The control that owns the popover, and the only thing that can open it. It stays visibly the source while the surface is up, and clicking it a second time closes what it opened.
2. Panel — A 210px surface on --bg with a --border-2 hairline and a long soft shadow — one of the few places in the system allowed elevation, because it genuinely floats above the page. It rises 4px over 180ms and never covers its own trigger.
3. Row — 14px Body in --dim, filling to --panel-2 with an --fg label on hover, at 9px by 11px so the whole width is a target. Every row acts and every row closes the popover; nothing here just changes what the popover looks like.
4. Divider — A single --border hairline with 5px of air either side, separating destructive rows from safe ones. It is the only structure a menu popover gets — no headings, no nested groups, no second divider.
5. Destructive row — Delete and its relatives, in #ff8f6b, always last and always below the divider. Choosing one opens a confirming modal rather than acting immediately — a surface this easy to dismiss cannot be trusted with an irreversible click.

### Variants

- Menu (--dim, --fg, --panel-2, --border, --alarm-soft): Three to seven actions on one object, each row closing the popover as it fires. It is the overflow valve for a row or a card: the two actions worth showing stay as buttons, the rest come here.
- Detail (--faint, --fg, --accent, --border-2): Facts about the anchor that are too long for a tooltip and too minor for a drawer — a run's timings, an operator's account. It may carry one link out, and no more.

A popover never scrolls, never nests a second popover and never holds a form with more than one field. Each of those is the same signal: the content has outgrown a peripheral surface and belongs in a Drawer.

### States

- Default: --dim, no fill.
- Hover: --panel-2, --fg label.
- Focus: 3px accent-soft ring.
- Destructive: Below the divider.

The four row states shown against the live demo's own "ROW STATES" swatches (archive/v1 lines 15997-16002), not the structured `popRules`/`popA11y` lists — see extractionNotes for why they're modelled here rather than folded into Rules.

### Use when

- A control owns three to seven actions that do not deserve permanent space.
- The operator needs a few facts about one thing without leaving the page.
- Abandoning the surface should cost nothing — no answer required, no state lost.
- The content is short enough to be read whole, with no scrolling.

### Use something else when

- modal: The operator must decide before continuing — that is a Modal.
- drawer: The content scrolls or is edited over time — that is a Drawer.
- tooltip: It is one short line explaining a control — that is a Tooltip.
- select: The rows set a single value on a field — that is Select.

### Content rules

- Rows are sentence-case verbs in Body 14px: "Rename", "Duplicate", "Archive", "Delete" — never uppercase Label, which is the tab and nav voice.
- Name the object only when the row is ambiguous without it: "Delete run" inside a page about one run is noise; on a table row it is necessary.
- Keep every row to two words. A row that needs a clause is an action with consequences, and the consequence belongs in the modal that follows.
- Detail popovers use uppercase Label field names in --faint with values in --fg, at most six pairs, and no paragraph of prose.
- One way out, at most: a single amber link at the foot of a detail popover. Two links make it a page in the wrong place.

### Examples

- [demo] Demo
- [good] Destructive below the divider — Destructive actions sit last, below a divider, so they cannot be hit on the way past.
- [bad] Destructive first — Never put Delete first or mix it in with the safe rows — one slip and the object is gone.
- [good] Anchored to its trigger — Anchored to its trigger with a 9px offset and aligned to its near edge.
- [bad] A menu with a scrollbar — Never give a popover a scrollbar — if the list is that long, it was a drawer.
- [good] Facts and one way out — A detail popover holds facts and at most one way out, in amber.
- [bad] A multi-field form — Never put a multi-field form in one — a surface you can lose by clicking away must not hold work.

### Accessibility

- Menu semantics: The trigger carries aria-haspopup and aria-expanded, and the panel is a role="menu" of role="menuitem" rows — so the number of actions is known before the operator starts walking them.
- Focus moves and returns: Focus enters the first row on open and returns to the trigger on close, however the popover was dismissed. Focus is not trapped: it is a peripheral surface, and Tab leaving it simply closes it.
- Escape and outside click: Escape closes it from anywhere, an outside click closes it without acting on what was clicked through, and the page keeps its scroll position. Nothing about dismissal needs to be learned.
- Destructive is spoken: A destructive row names its object in the accessible name and points at the modal that follows, so a screen-reader user knows a confirm is coming rather than fearing the row itself.

### Tokens

- --bg: Panel surface.
- --border-2: Panel hairline.
- --border: Row divider.
- --dim, --fg: Rows at rest and on hover.
- --panel-2: Row hover fill.
- --accent-soft: Row focus ring.
- --alarm-soft: Destructive row highlight.
- --faint, --accent: Detail field labels and its one link out.

### Related

- modal (often-confused-with): A modal must be answered and stops the page; a popover can be walked away from. A destructive row here always hands over to one.
- tooltip (often-confused-with): Tooltips open on hover and hold one unreachable line. The moment the content contains something to click, it has to be a popover.
- select (contrasts-with): Select uses the same floating surface to set one value on a field. Its rows change state rather than perform work, which is why it is a control and this is a menu.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (24 Aug 2026): Scrolling panels, nested popovers and multi-field forms ruled out; destructive rows fixed below the divider.
- v1.0.1 (16 Aug 2026): Offset standardised at 9px with edge-aware flipping on all four placements.
- v1.0.0 (8 Aug 2026): Popover introduced at 210px with menu and detail kinds and a 180ms rise.

## Progress

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 2 Oct 2026 · /components/progress

Purpose: Reports a measured fraction of a known total, and nothing else.

### Description

Progress reports a measured fraction of a known total, and nothing else.

The whole component rests on one condition: the system honestly knows the denominator. That is the line against Loading — while the total is unknown the answer is a phase label and a sweep, and the moment it becomes knowable this takes over. A bar that fakes a fraction is worse than no bar at all, because the operator plans around it.

### Anatomy

1. Label — What is being counted, in 12.5px --dim sentence case: "Exporting runs". It names the work rather than the state, so the bar is legible the second the operator glances at it.
2. Value — The measured fraction in --mute, written as a count wherever a count exists — 132 / 214 rather than 62%. A percentage is a derived number; the count is the thing the operator can act on.
3. Fill — --accent at 85% opacity, animating its width over 300ms so a jump of several percent reads as movement rather than a redraw. It only ever moves forward.
4. Track — A 5px --panel-2 bar, square-cornered like everything else, spanning the full width of its container. Its length is the denominator made visible, which is why it is never sized to the content.
5. Caption — One optional 11px --faint line under the bar, in the // phase voice, for what the fraction cannot say: which shard is being written, how much time is left. Present only when it is true.

### Variants

- Bar (--panel-2, --accent): One long task with a countable total — 132 of 214 runs exported. The default, and the only variant allowed to carry an estimate of time remaining.
- Steps (--accent, --panel-2): A pipeline with named stages, where being halfway through stage two is not information the operator can use. Segments fill whole; they never fill partially.
- Meter (--panel-2, --accent): A quantity inside a table row or a card, where the surrounding row already names it — quota used, coverage, capacity. It reports a level, not necessarily work in flight.

There is no indeterminate bar and no spinner. A bar that animates without a denominator is a lie told smoothly — that case belongs to Loading, which says what the system is doing instead of pretending to know how far along it is.

### Use when

- The system can count both what is done and what is left.
- The work runs long enough that the operator would otherwise wonder — roughly five seconds and up.
- The fraction is a level worth knowing on its own: quota, coverage, capacity.
- The stages are named and discrete, and finishing one is the news.

### Use something else when

- loading: The total is unknown — that is Loading, with a phase label.
- toast: The result is already in and only needs reporting — that is a Toast.

### Content rules

- The label is a present participle naming the work: "Exporting runs", "Indexing documents" — never "Loading", never "Please wait".
- Write the value as a count with the total: 132 / 214. Percentages are for continuous quantities, and then with no decimal places.
- Time estimates are approximate and say so — "~3M LEFT" — and they only appear once the rate has settled enough to be worth printing.
- The caption uses the // phase voice in uppercase mono, matching Loading, so the two components read as one system when a task moves between them.
- On completion say what finished, in the past tense and with the number — "214 runs exported" — then let the bar go.

### Examples

- [demo] Bar
- [demo] Steps
- [demo] Meter
- [good] A real count beside the bar — A real count beside the bar, so the fraction can be checked against something.
- [bad] Invented decimals and “Working…” — Never invent decimals or say "Working" — false precision over a vague label fools nobody twice.
- [good] Steps fill whole segments — Steps fill whole segments — stage two is either done or it is not.
- [bad] A part-filled segment — Never part-fill a segment — if the inside of a stage is measurable, use a bar.
- [good] On failure the fill holds its position — On failure the fill holds its position and turns, so the operator sees how far it got.
- [bad] Resetting to zero on failure — Never reset the bar to zero on failure — the work that did happen is the useful part.

### Accessibility

- Progressbar with values: role="progressbar" carrying aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax, labelled by the visible label. Meters use role="meter", because a level is not work in flight.
- Announced in steps: The value is announced at coarse intervals — roughly every 10% or on each stage change — not on every tick. A bar that speaks per frame is a bar nobody can listen to.
- Colour is never alone: The fill is always paired with a count or percentage in text, and failure is stated in words as well as in #ff8f6b. Amber over --panel-2 measures 5.8:1, but the number is what carries the meaning.
- Reduced motion: Under prefers-reduced-motion the width snaps instead of animating. The value still updates on the same schedule, so nothing about the reading is lost with the movement.

### Tokens

- --panel-2: Track
- --accent: Fill while running
- --accent: Fill at completion
- --dim, --mute: Label and value
- --mute: Phase caption

### Related

- loading (contrasts-with): Where work goes while the total is unknown. The two hand over to each other mid-task, which is why they share the // caption voice.
- table (composes-with): Meters live in table rows to compare levels down a column, which is why the inline variant carries no label of its own.
- toast (contrasts-with): The bar reports work in flight; the toast reports that it finished. When the count reaches the total, one replaces the other.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (24 Aug 2026): Indeterminate bars and spinners ruled out; failure now freezes the fill instead of resetting it.
- v1.0.1 (18 Aug 2026): Counts made the default value format, with percentages reserved for continuous quantities.
- v1.0.0 (10 Aug 2026): Bar, steps and meter variants introduced on a 5px track with a 300ms advance.

---

## Radio

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 24 Aug 2026 · /components/radio

Purpose: A set of mutually exclusive options, all visible at once, exactly one of them chosen.

### Description

A radio group is a set of mutually exclusive options, all visible at once, exactly one of them chosen.

It exists so the operator can compare the alternatives before committing, which is why it costs vertical space and why it stops being the right control past about five options. The line against Checkbox is arithmetic: checkboxes are independent and can all be off, radios are one-of and can never be none. If “none” is a legitimate answer, it has to be an option in the list rather than an empty group.

### Anatomy

1. Group — The set itself, and the real unit of the component — a radio never exists alone. Options stack one per line with 2px between rows, so the eye reads a list rather than a layout.
2. Dial — An 18px circle with a 1.5px border, fixed at every density. Round is reserved: with dots and avatars, this is one of the only circles in a system that is otherwise square, and the shape is what says one-of.
3. Dot — A 9px --accent disc fading in over 160ms, centred in the dial. It fills rather than ticks, because a tick is the checkbox’s word for "yes" and this control answers "which".
4. Label — 14px Body in --fg, sentence case, and part of the target. It is the option itself — never a description of the dial — and it may carry one --mute line underneath when the trade-off needs stating.
5. Hit row — Dial and label share one row padded 9px by 11px, so the whole line is clickable and clears the minimum target in dense chrome. Hover fills the row with --panel-2, never just the dial.

### States

- Off: Not chosen. The dial is empty rather than dimmed, because a faint dot would read as a weak choice instead of no choice.
- On: The chosen option: amber ring, amber 9px dot fading in over 160ms. Exactly one row in the group is ever in this state.
- Error: A required group submitted with nothing chosen. Every dial in the group takes the border, since the fault belongs to the question and not to one option.
- Disabled: An option that cannot be chosen right now. It keeps its dot if it was the selection, and something next to the group has to say why it is locked.

There is no indeterminate radio and no way to clear a group by clicking the selected option again. Both would mean a group with nothing chosen, which is the one state a radio set is not allowed to be in — add an explicit option instead.

### Use when

- Two to five options, exactly one of which will be true.
- The options need comparing before choosing — seeing them all is the point.
- The choice is part of a form and commits with everything else.
- The wording of each option matters more than the space it costs.

### Use something else when

- select: Six or more options, or a list that grows — that is Select.
- checkbox: Several can be true at once — that is Checkbox.
- switch: It is one setting on or off, committing instantly — that is a Switch.
- chip: The choice filters a list rather than setting a value — those are Chips.

### Content rules

- Options are sentence case and grammatically parallel: "Every run", "Failures only", "Never" — never a mix of nouns and clauses.
- Name the outcome, not the mechanism: "Failures only" rather than "Filter where status equals failed".
- Keep options roughly the same length. One option twice as long as the others reads as the recommended one whether you meant it or not.
- Add at most one --mute line under an option, and only where the trade-off is not obvious from the label — "Skips validation".
- The group needs a question above it in --dim: "Notify me about" — short, no colon, and never repeated inside the options.

### Examples

- [demo] Ingest or normalize
- [good] A default already chosen — “Never” written as an option, stacked one per line, with one already chosen.
- [bad] A group with nothing chosen — Never leave a group empty — the operator cannot tell a missing default from a broken form.
- [good] One setting, two states is a Switch — One setting with two states is a switch, and commits the moment it is flipped.
- [bad] Two rows saying on and off — Never spend two rows saying on and off — that is a switch wearing a radio group.
- [good] A clarifying line per option — One clarifying line per option, in --mute, when the trade-off is not obvious.
- [bad] A group wrapped into a grid — Never wrap a group into a grid — the reading order stops being obvious and so does the set.

### Accessibility

- One tab stop: The group is a role="radiogroup" labelled by its question, and the whole set is a single tab stop — Tab enters at the chosen option and Tab again leaves the group entirely.
- Arrows choose: Arrow keys move between options and select as they move, which is the expected behaviour and the reason radios must not have side effects. Space selects the focused option where nothing is chosen yet.
- Colour is never alone: Selection is the filled dot as well as the amber ring, and it is carried in aria-checked. Amber on --panel measures 6.6:1, but the dot is what reads for anyone who cannot separate the hues.
- Locked options explain: A disabled option keeps its label readable and is described by the same text that says why it is locked, so the reason is announced with the option rather than sitting somewhere else on screen.

### Tokens

- --border-2: Dial at rest
- --accent: Chosen ring and dot
- --fg: Option labels
- --mute: Clarifying line under an option
- --panel-2: Row hover fill
- --alarm-line: Error border

### Related

- checkbox (alternative): Checkboxes are independent and can all be off. If the answers are not mutually exclusive, the square is the right shape.
- select (alternative): Past five options the list should collapse into a field. Select trades comparing the options for getting the space back.
- switch (alternative): A switch is one setting with two states, committing instantly. Two radios saying on and off is always a switch in disguise.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (24 Aug 2026): Clearing a group by re-clicking ruled out; error state moved to every dial in the group rather than one.
- v1.0.1 (20 Aug 2026): Hit row extended to the label with a --panel-2 hover fill across the whole line.
- v1.0.0 (12 Aug 2026): Radio introduced at an 18px dial with a 9px dot and a 160ms fade.

---

## Scrollbar

Status: stable · Version: 1.0.0 · Updated: 2 Oct 2026 · /components/scrollbar

Purpose: The browser's own scroll control, restyled to two greys — never a custom-built replacement.

### Description

A scrollbar is the browser's own control, restyled to two greys — never a custom-built replacement.

It exists so any pane that overflows can be scrolled without inventing a new way to do it. That is the boundary against a Progress bar or any other painted indicator: this shell is never drawn by the system, only recoloured — the browser keeps every native behaviour, and the design keeps only the two colours it is allowed to change.

### Anatomy

1. Thumb — A 4px pill inset inside the 10px lane by a 3px transparent border, so it never touches the page edge. --border-2 at rest, --mute on hover — the only two states it has.
2. Track — Transparent underneath the thumb, always. It never grows a fill, a hairline, or a hover state of its own — the page edge is the only boundary it needs.

### States

- Default: Present but quiet — visible enough to find, quiet enough to ignore while reading.
- Hover: One step up the grey ramp for as long as the pointer is over the thumb or the track beside it. No transition is timed; the browser owns the swap.

### Use when

- Any pane, list, or dock column can overflow and the browser already knows how to scroll it.

### Use something else when

- progress: The value being shown is a quantity, not a scroll position — that is Progress.
- main-rail: The column is the 56px collapsed rail — MainNav hides this control there instead of shrinking it further.

### Content rules

- Width is fixed at 10px everywhere — content panes, the subnav rail, modals. There is no thin or thick variant to choose between.
- Radius is 2px, matching the system lock. The thumb never grows a pointed or pill shape of its own.
- The corner where a vertical and horizontal track meet is always transparent — it never draws a swatch.
- Firefox gets the same two greys through scrollbar-color rather than a separate design; the two engines must always resolve to one look.
- The main rail's own list (.dock-scroll) hides this control entirely rather than restyling it — a 56px column has no room to spare for a lane.

### Examples

- [demo] Panel
- [good] Thin and quiet — Thin, grey, and nearly invisible until the pointer is on it.
- [bad] Widened and coloured — Never widen or colour the thumb to draw attention — it competes with the content it's meant to stay out of the way of.

### Accessibility

- Native, not custom: This is the browser's own scrollbar, restyled through the two standard pseudo-element and scrollbar-color hooks — never a JS-built replacement. Keyboard scrolling, wheel, trackpad and OS gestures all keep working exactly as the platform defines them.
- Colour never alone: The hover state changes lightness (--border-2 to --mute), not hue, so it reads under any colour-vision deficiency and in either theme.
- Hit target is the OS default: The visual thumb is 4px, but the browser's own scrollbar hit area — wider than what is painted — is untouched, so pointer users never lose the margin for error the platform already gives them.
- No motion to reduce: The thumb has no transition or animation of its own; hover is an instant colour swap, so prefers-reduced-motion has nothing here to turn off.

### Tokens

- --border-2: Thumb at rest
- --mute: Thumb on hover

### Related

- table (composes-with): The component most often responsible for a horizontal thumb appearing at all — a wide row set is what puts this control to work.
- main-rail (contrasts-with): Hides this exact control on its own item list, because a 56px collapsed rail has no width left to give it.

### Changelog

- v1.0.0 (20 Sept 2026): Documented as its own component: 10px lane, 4px inset thumb, two states, and the corner rule that keeps it out of every layout's way.

---

## Select

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 8 Oct 2026 · /components/select

Purpose: A select collapses one choice out of many into a single field, and spends a click to get the space back.

### Description

A select collapses one choice out of many into a single field, and spends a click to get the space back.

It is the same one-of-many question a Radio group asks, traded the other way round: the options are hidden until asked for, so the field always shows the current answer and never the alternatives. That trade is worth making from about six options up, or whenever the list can grow after launch. Below that, hiding the choices costs the operator more than the rows would.

### Anatomy

1. Field — The closed control, and the only part visible most of the time. It shares the text input’s box exactly — same height, same 10px/13px padding, same 2px corner — so a form of mixed controls still reads as one row of boxes.
2. Value — The current answer in 14px --fg, or the placeholder in --mute when nothing is chosen. It is always the chosen option’s own words, never a count or a summary, because the field is the only place that answer appears.
3. Caret — A single glyph on the right that rotates 180° and turns amber while the menu is open. It is the whole affordance: there is no second button, and the entire field is the hit target.
4. Menu — A floating listbox on --bg with a --border-2 hairline and the deep panel shadow, matched to the field’s width and anchored 4px below it. It flips above the field when the viewport is short rather than scrolling the page.
5. Option — One value per 9px/11px row, with an amber tick on the current one and a --panel-2 fill under hover and keyboard focus alike. Selecting closes the menu — a select commits on the click.

### States

- Default: Closed with a value. This is the state the field lives in, so the value has to be legible at a glance and never abbreviated.
- Placeholder: Nothing chosen yet. The text is a verb phrase in --mute so it never reads as a value, and it is never the field’s label doing double duty.
- Hover: Pointer anywhere on the field. The border lifts to --fg and the caret follows, confirming the whole box is the target rather than the glyph.
- Focus: Reached by keyboard, menu still closed. The soft amber ring is the system focus treatment and appears on nothing else.
- Open: Menu showing. The field keeps the amber border for as long as the menu is up, so the two read as one object even with the shadow between them.
- Error: A required field submitted empty. The border and caret both turn, and a line of text underneath says which field and why — colour never carries it alone.
- Disabled: Not changeable now. The value stays readable at 45% so the operator can still see what it is set to, and something adjacent explains what would unlock it.

There is no read-only variant distinct from disabled, and no searchable variant. Past roughly twenty options the field stops being the answer and the choice belongs in a modal picker with real search, rather than a select that quietly grows a text input.

### Use when

- Six or more options, exactly one of which will be true.
- The list is data rather than design — it can grow without a redesign.
- The chosen value matters more day to day than the alternatives do.
- The row is dense — a toolbar or a table filter — and rows are not available.

### Use something else when

- radio: Two to five options that want comparing — that is a Radio group.
- select-multi: Several values can be true at once — that is Select (Multi).
- popover: The rows are commands rather than values — that is a Popover menu.
- chip: The choice narrows a visible list — those are Chips.

### Content rules

- Label the field with the noun it sets — Stage, Owner, Region — above the box, never inside it as a placeholder that vanishes on the first pick.
- Write the placeholder as an instruction rather than a value: “Choose a stage”, not “None”, which is itself a legitimate option and would be ambiguous.
- Keep options to two or three words in sentence case, and make them parallel — all nouns or all verbs — so the list scans as one set of alternatives.
- Order options the way the operator thinks: by pipeline order, frequency or size, and only alphabetically when the list is long and unordered by nature.
- If “None” or “Any” is a real answer, put it in the list as the first row rather than relying on an empty field to mean it.

### Examples

- [demo] Stage select
- [good] Label above, value in the field — Label above, the current value in the field — readable without opening anything.
- [bad] Label doing duty as the placeholder — Never let the label do duty as the placeholder — once a value is picked, the question is gone.
- [good] A required field that says so in words — An empty required field says so in words underneath, not in the border alone.
- [bad] Two selects of two options each — Never stack two selects that each hold two options — that is two radio groups paying rent on a click each.

### Accessibility

- Combobox and listbox: The field is a role="combobox" with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at the role="listbox" menu; each row is an option carrying aria-selected. The field is labelled by the visible label, not by placeholder text.
- Keyboard opens and moves: Enter, Space or Down opens the menu at the current value; arrows move the active option, Enter commits, Escape closes and returns focus to the field with the old value intact. Tab closes and moves on — it never leaves an orphaned menu behind.
- Focus and selection differ: The active row under the keyboard and the currently selected row are two different things, so the tick marks selection while the --panel-2 fill marks position. Never let the fill alone imply what is chosen.
- Errors are announced: The message under the field is tied to it with aria-describedby and the field takes aria-invalid, so a screen reader hears the reason with the control rather than as a loose sentence somewhere in the form.

### Tokens

- --border-2: Resting field border, menu hairline
- --accent-line: Field border while focused or open
- --accent: Caret when open, tick on the current option
- --bg: Field and menu surface
- --panel-2: Hover and active-option fill
- --mute: Placeholder text, resting caret
- --alarm-line: Error border

### Related

- radio (alternative): Use instead under about six options. A radio group spends rows to show the alternatives; a select spends a click to hide them.
- select-multi (often-confused-with): Differs in that the menu stays open and the chosen set becomes tokens in the field. One value or many is the only question that decides between them.
- popover (often-confused-with): Looks the same open, but its rows are actions that do something. If a row does not set the field’s value, it belongs in a popover menu.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Menu width locked to the field; searchable and read-only variants ruled out in favour of a modal picker past twenty options.
- v1.0.1 (21 Aug 2026): Selection now closes the menu; active-row fill separated from the selected tick.
- v1.0.0 (13 Aug 2026): Select introduced as a custom listbox sharing the text input’s box.

---

## Select (Multi)

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 8 Oct 2026 · /components/select-multi

Purpose: A multi-select holds several values in one field, each one a token the operator can take back out.

### Description

A multi-select holds several values in one field, each one a token the operator can take back out.

Everything it does differently from Select follows from one fact: the answer is a set, so the set has to stay visible and stay editable. That is why picking does not close the menu, why the chosen values come back as removable tokens rather than as a count, and why the field is allowed to be taller than a text input. It is still a form control, not a filter bar — if the choice narrows a list in front of the operator, those are Chips.

### Anatomy

1. Field — A fixed 42px box — four pixels taller than the single select, and never taller than that. The height is fixed on purpose: a field that grows a row per pick reflows the form underneath the operator while they are working in it.
2. Token — One chosen value, in the amber-soft box with an --accent-line hairline, carrying its own ✕. The tokens are the answer, which is why they name their values in full and are never collapsed into “3 selected”.
3. Overflow — A counted --panel-2 chip standing in for the tokens that no longer fit the measured width. It is the pressure valve that lets the field stay one row tall, and opening the menu shows the full set again.
4. Menu — The same listbox as Select — field width, --border-2 hairline, deep shadow — with a square 16px checkbox on every row and its metadata right-aligned in --faint. Picking does not close it, because the answer is a set and sets are built up.
5. Footer — A hairline-separated row with the live count on the left and ALL / CLEAR on the right. It exists because bulk moves are the two things a multi-select is asked for that a single select never is.

### States

- Empty: No values yet. The placeholder is a plural instruction — “Select stages” — so it reads as a prompt for a set rather than for one value.
- Focus: Reached by keyboard with the menu still closed. The field takes the soft amber ring, and the caret turns amber the moment the menu opens.
- Overflow: More tokens chosen than fit the measured width. The remainder becomes one counted chip rather than a second row, and the count is exact.
- Error: A required field submitted with an empty set. The border and caret turn and a line underneath says how many are needed — never the border alone.
- Disabled: Not editable now. Tokens stay legible but lose their ✕, so the set can still be read while nothing about it can be changed.

There is no state for a partially valid set and no per-token error. Validation belongs to the field as a whole, because the operator submits a set rather than a sequence of picks — and the specimens for every state are rendered live in the panel below.

### Use when

- Several values out of seven or more can be true at once.
- The chosen set has to stay readable after the menu closes.
- Values are removed as often as they are added — tokens make that one click.
- The list is data and can grow, so a column of checkboxes would not hold.

### Use something else when

- select: Exactly one value is allowed — that is Select.
- checkbox: Under about seven options with room for rows — those are Checkboxes.
- chip: The set narrows a list already on screen — those are Chips.
- popover: The rows run commands rather than setting values — that is a Popover menu.

### Content rules

- Label the field with the plural noun it collects — Stages, Owners, Regions — so the operator knows a set is expected before they open it.
- Write the placeholder as a plural instruction: “Select stages”, never “Stage” or “None selected”, which read as a single value and a state respectively.
- Keep option labels to two or three words, since each one has to survive being shown twice — once as a menu row, once as a token in a narrow field.
- Show metadata in the menu rows rather than on the tokens: the row is where the operator decides, and the token only has to identify what was decided.
- Count in the footer with the total — “3 of 5” — so the operator can see at a glance whether ALL would change anything.

### Examples

- [demo] Stage multi-select
- [good] Fixed height, counted overflow — Fixed height: tokens that no longer fit collapse into a counted overflow chip.
- [bad] A field that grows row by row — Never let the field grow row by row — the form reflows under the operator as they pick.
- [bad] Dials in a multi-select menu — Never use dials in a multi-select menu — round means one-of everywhere else in the system.
- [bad] The set replaced by a count — Never replace the set with a count — the operator has to reopen the menu to learn what they chose.

### Accessibility

- Multiselectable listbox: The field is a role="combobox" with aria-expanded; the menu is a role="listbox" with aria-multiselectable and each row carries aria-checked. The plural label is what the field is named by, not the placeholder.
- The menu stays put: Space toggles the active row and leaves the menu open and focus where it was, so a keyboard operator builds the set in one pass. Escape closes and returns focus to the field with the set intact; Tab closes and moves on.
- Tokens are reachable: Each ✕ is a real button labelled “Remove Ingest” rather than a bare glyph, and Backspace with the field focused removes the last token — the shortcut is a convenience, never the only way.
- Changes are announced: The count line is a live region, so adding or clearing values is spoken as “3 of 5 selected” instead of leaving a keyboard operator to infer the state from a field they cannot see.

### Tokens

- --accent-line: Token border, field border when open
- --accent-soft: Token fill
- --accent: Caret when open, checked box fill
- --border-2: Resting field border, menu hairline, overflow chip
- --panel-2: Overflow chip fill, row hover
- --mute: Placeholder, token remove glyph
- --alarm-line: Error border

### Related

- select (often-confused-with): Differs only in cardinality, and everything else follows: one value, so the menu closes on the pick and the field shows a word instead of tokens.
- checkbox (alternative): Use instead under about seven options. Rows of boxes cost space but no clicks, and they show the whole set of possibilities at once.
- chip (often-confused-with): Looks like the tokens but does the opposite job: chips narrow a list in front of the operator and commit nothing to a form.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Field height locked at 42px with measured overflow collapse; footer count paired with the total.
- v1.0.1 (22 Aug 2026): Selection no longer closes the menu; ALL and CLEAR added to the footer.
- v1.0.0 (14 Aug 2026): Multi introduced with removable tokens and square boxes in the menu.

## Navigation (Subnav)

Status: stable · Version: 1.0.0 · Updated: 5 Oct 2026 · /components/subnav

Purpose: The column of pages inside one workspace, docked to the right of the main rail. The one navigation that changes with the route.

### Description

The subnav is the column of pages inside one workspace, docked to the right of the main rail.

It is the only navigation in the product that changes with the route: a different workspace means a different list, and the list is the workspace's own table of contents. The line against Navigation (Tabs) is what happens when you click. A subnav row loads a different page, with its own URL and its own header; a tab swaps the view of the page you are already on. If leaving the row would lose unsaved work in the panel beside it, it was a tab.

### Anatomy

1. Column — A 214px column docked against the main rail and sticky to the top of the scroll container, so a long page never scrolls its own navigation away. It sits inside the content area because it belongs to the workspace, not to the app.
2. Section row — A group of pages, set as a Label at 12px and .14em uppercase, and clickable in its own right — it opens the section landing page and expands its children. Only one section is open at a time.
3. Count — The number of pages the section owns, right-aligned in --faint. It is present only where it is true and absent where a section has no children, which is what keeps it readable as information rather than decoration.
4. Child list — The expanded pages, indented 12px behind a single --border hairline and set in sentence case at 12.5px. That hairline is the only nesting device in the component, and it is never drawn twice.
5. Active page — The current route, marked with an --accent label on a --panel-2 fill while its parent section keeps the 2px amber rail at the column edge. Two amber marks, one statement: this section, that page.

### Variants

- Section (--fg, --panel-2): A group of pages that belong together, and itself a destination — clicking it opens the section's own landing page and expands its children. Only one section is ever expanded, so the column's height stays predictable as the operator moves.
- Page (--accent, --panel-2): One route inside the section, indented behind a hairline. The case change from uppercase to sentence case is what tells the two levels apart — not the indent, which disappears the moment the label wraps.

There is no third level. A page that needs children of its own has outgrown the subnav: give it tabs inside its own header, or promote the section to a workspace on the main rail.

### States

- Default: --mute label, no fill.
- Hover: --panel-2 fill, --fg label.
- Active: Amber label, amber rail.
- Focus: 2px accent ring.

### Use when

- A page inside this workspace with its own route and its own page header.
- Something the operator will want to reach without going through another page first.
- A section that owns two or more pages — one child alone is just the section.
- A destination that stays put: the subnav is per workspace, not per record.

### Use something else when

- main-rail: Another workspace — that is Navigation (Main).
- tabs: A view of the page already open — that is Navigation (Tabs).
- chip: A filter over a list — those are Chips above the table.
- button: Anything that performs work — that is a Button in the page header.

### Content rules

- Sections are one or two words, uppercase, plural where they name a set: OPERATIONS, RESEARCH, ARCHIVE — never a verb and never a sentence.
- Pages are sentence case and name the thing, not the act: "Live vessels", "Crew roster" — not "View vessels" and not "Vessel management".
- Keep a page label under about 22 characters so it holds one line at 214px; if it cannot, the page is really two pages or the name is a description.
- Never repeat the workspace in a row — inside Fleet the page is "Maintenance", not "Fleet maintenance". The header already said where you are.
- Counts are plain integers. No "12 new", no plus signs, no dots: the subnav says how much exists, never how much has changed.

### Examples

- [demo] Navigation (Subnav)
- [good] One section open — Only one section is ever expanded, so the column's height stays predictable.
- [bad] A third level of nesting — There is no third level. A page that needs children has outgrown the subnav.
- [good] Case signals the level — Uppercase sections, sentence-case pages — the case change tells the two levels apart.
- [bad] Indent as the only signal — Never rely on indent alone — it disappears the moment a label wraps.

### Accessibility

- Nav landmark, per workspace: The column is a nav landmark labelled with the workspace name, so a screen-reader user meeting two nav landmarks can tell the rail from the pages without exploring either.
- Current page, spoken: The active page carries aria-current="page" and the open section aria-expanded. The amber rail and the amber label are the visual half of the same statement, never the whole of it.
- Colour is never alone: Active state is signalled three ways at once: the rail, the --accent label and aria-current. Amber against --panel-2 measures 6.4:1, but the marker is what carries it for anyone who cannot see the hue.
- Reading order matches sight: Sections and their children follow the DOM in the order they are drawn, and the hidden stub keeps its button in place — collapsing the column changes its width, never its position in the tab order.

### Tokens

- --panel-2: Row hover and active fill
- --accent: Active rail and active page label
- --mute: Resting pages and section labels
- --border: Child-list hairline and stub edge
- --faint: Section counts

### Related

- main-rail (contrasts-with): The rail chooses the workspace this column belongs to. It never nests, which is exactly the job it hands over here.
- tabs (often-confused-with): Tabs swap the view of one page without a route change. If clicking would keep you on the same page, it was never a subnav row.
- header (composes-with): The page header names the row you just clicked. The subnav marks where you are; the header confirms it.

### Changelog

- v1.0.0 (5 Oct 2026): Navigation (Subnav) ported: two-level sections/pages, one section open at a time, sticky 214px column with a hide/show stub.
- v0.1.0 (4 Oct 2026): Draft stub created so Tabs' own relationship had somewhere real to point.

---

## Switch

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 25 Aug 2026 · /components/switch

Purpose: Turns one setting on or off, and the change takes effect the moment it moves.

### Description

A switch turns one thing on or off, and the change takes effect the moment it moves.

That instant commit is the entire difference from a Checkbox, which records an answer and waits for a submit. A switch has no submit to wait for, so it belongs in settings and toolbars rather than in forms, and it must never appear beside a Save button that implies it was holding its breath. It is also always one thing: two switches offered as alternatives are a Radio group in the wrong clothes.

### Anatomy

1. Track — A 40×22 pill with a 1px border — the one shape in the system allowed a 20px radius, because the rounded ends are what make it read as a thing that slides rather than a box that fills. Amber fill means on; --panel-2 means off.
2. Knob — A 16px circle travelling 18px in 180ms. The movement is the feedback: it is the only control here that animates its own state change rather than fading between two paints.
3. Label — A stative phrase naming what is true when the switch is on — "Auto-retry failed runs", never "Turn on auto-retry". Commands belong on buttons; a switch describes a condition.
4. Hit row — The whole row is the target, so label, sub-line and track all toggle. It gives a 44px-tall hit area out of a 22px control and takes --panel-2 on hover across the full width.
5. Sub-line — One optional 12px --mute line for the consequence, present only when the label cannot carry it: what happens when on, or what would unlock a disabled row. Never a restatement of the label.

### States

- Off: The resting negative. The track is a filled --panel-2 rather than an empty outline, so off still reads as a deliberate position rather than a control that failed to load.
- On: Amber track, knob at the right. Amber means act everywhere in the system, and this is the one place it also means "is acting" — the setting is live right now.
- Hover: Pointer anywhere on the row. The border and knob lift together so it is clear the whole row is pressable, not just the pill.
- Focus: Reached by keyboard. The ring sits around the track rather than the row, so the operator sees which control they are about to commit.
- Disabled off: Cannot be turned on right now. The row dims as one piece and the sub-line says what would unlock it — never a tooltip alone.
- Disabled on: On and locked, usually by policy. The amber drains out so nothing dimmed ever reads as active, but the knob stays right so the state is still legible.

There is no indeterminate switch and no loading switch. If the change takes long enough to need a spinner, the control is a Button and the outcome belongs in a snackbar — a switch that moves and then moves back is worse than one that never moved.

### Use when

- One setting has two states and the change applies immediately.
- The effect is reversible with the same gesture that caused it.
- The row lives in settings, a toolbar, or a panel — somewhere with no submit.
- Both states are legitimate resting places, not a task to be completed.

### Use something else when

- checkbox: The answer is submitted with a form — that is a Checkbox.
- radio: There are more than two states, or two named alternatives — that is a Radio group.
- button: The action runs once and finishes — that is a Button.
- badge: The state is assigned by the system and only reported — that is a Badge.

### Content rules

- Write the label as the state, not the action: "Auto-retry failed runs". If it reads like a button, it will be treated like one.
- Never label the two ends of the track. The knob position and the amber fill carry on and off; ON/OFF text next to them is a second, competing answer.
- Keep the label under about six words and put the consequence in the sub-line, so a column of switches stays scannable as a list of settings.
- Say what a locked switch needs in the sub-line — "Needs an admin on the workspace" — rather than leaving the operator to hover for a reason.
- Confirm nothing on toggle. If the change deserves feedback beyond the knob moving, that is a snackbar, and if it deserves a confirm dialog it is not a switch.

### Examples

- [demo] Auto-retry failed runs
- [good] A stative label with its consequence — A stative label naming what is on, and one --mute line for the consequence.
- [bad] A command label flanked by ON/OFF — Never write the label as a command, and never flank the track with ON/OFF — the knob says which it is.
- [good] Independent settings stacked — Independent settings stack as rows with the tracks aligned on one right-hand column.
- [bad] Two switches as alternatives — Never use two switches as alternatives — naming two options one-of is a radio group's job.
- [good] A locked switch explains itself — A locked switch keeps its label and says, in the sub-line, what would unlock it.
- [bad] A switch behind a Save button — Never put a switch behind a Save — it already committed, and the button makes the operator doubt it.

### Accessibility

- Role and state: The control is role="switch" with aria-checked, labelled by the visible label and described by the sub-line. Role switch rather than checkbox is what tells a screen reader the change has already happened.
- Space toggles: The row is one tab stop and Space toggles it; Enter does nothing, since the row is not a button. The whole row being the hit target means pointer and keyboard land on the same thing.
- Colour is never alone: On is the knob at the right as well as the amber track, and amber on --panel measures 6.6:1. Anyone who cannot see the fill still reads the position, which is why the knob travels the full 18px.
- No motion, no problem: Under prefers-reduced-motion the knob jumps rather than slides. The state is carried by position, so removing the transition costs nothing at all.

### Tokens

- --accent: Track fill when on
- --accent-line: Track border when on
- --panel-2: Track fill when off, row hover
- --border-2: Track border when off
- --dim: Knob when off
- --bg: Knob when on

### Related

- checkbox (alternative): Use instead inside a form. The square records an answer and waits for the submit; the pill has already changed the system.
- radio (alternative): Use instead when two named alternatives are being compared. A switch has no vocabulary for its off state beyond "not on".
- button (alternative): Use instead when the thing runs once and finishes. A switch describes a standing condition, never an errand.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Hit row extended across label and sub-line; loading and indeterminate switches ruled out.
- v1.0.1 (19 Aug 2026): Disabled-on drains the amber to --border-2 so nothing dimmed reads as active.
- v1.0.0 (12 Aug 2026): Switch introduced at 40×22 with a 16px knob and a 180ms travel.
