## Table

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 25 Aug 2026 · /components/table

Purpose: A list of records the operator works on, not a grid of numbers they read.

### Description

A table is a list of records the operator works on, not a grid of numbers they read.

Every decision here follows from that: rows are selectable, actions live on the row and in a toolbar that changes when a selection exists, and the columns are the few facts needed to decide which row to act on. It is the densest component in the system, so it is the one place where hover reveals rather than decorates. If the content is a matrix of measurements to be compared rather than records to be acted on, that is a Visualization problem, not this component.

### Anatomy

1. Header row — Column names in 10.5px --faint at .16em, sitting above a single hairline. They are labels rather than buttons: nothing in the header is amber, because the header describes the table and never acts on it.
2. Select column — A fixed 26px column holding the 18px square box, header included. It is first because selection precedes every bulk action, and its width is reserved whether or not the table is selectable, so rows never shift when selection is turned on.
3. Cell — One fact, one alignment rule: text left, numbers and times right, the record's name at 14px --fg and everything secondary at 12px --mute. Truncation with an ellipsis is allowed on the name only — every other column must fit.
4. Row — The unit of work: a 54px-tall band — 11px of padding around a 32px action box, content-driven rather than fixed — that takes --panel-2 on hover and, when selected, an --accent-2 tint with a 2px ice rail down its left edge. The rail is what makes a selection legible while scrolling a long body.
5. Row actions — A right-aligned cluster in a reserved column: the two or three frequent verbs as icons, then an overflow ⋯ for the rest. It fades in on hover and on keyboard focus, and the column is always there so the grid never reflows.

### States

- Toolbar — idle: With nothing selected: the row count on the left in --faint, then EXPORT and the one amber CREATE on the right. It is the table's title bar, so it never scrolls away from the body it counts.
- Toolbar — selection: The moment a row is checked, the same 56px band swaps to an ice count chip, the bulk verbs, and CLEAR. Swapping in place rather than stacking a second bar keeps the body from jumping under the operator's cursor.
- Row — default: Resting. Only the hairline under the header separates rows; there are no zebra stripes, because 44px of height and one hover fill already do the work without adding a second rhythm.
- Row — hover: The whole band fills and the action icons fade in. This is the one component where hover reveals rather than decorates, which is why every revealed action also has a keyboard path.
- Row — selected: Ice tint plus the 2px rail, held whether or not the pointer is on the row. Selection outranks hover: a selected row under the cursor keeps the ice rather than the grey.
- Row — menu open: The row raises above its siblings so the overflow panel is not clipped, and the ⋯ trigger stays filled for as long as the menu is up, so the operator can see which row they are aimed at.

### Use when

- Rows are records with a stable identity the operator acts on.
- The same action is often wanted on several rows at once.
- Four to seven facts per row decide what to do next.
- Scanning down one column is a real task — status, owner, last run.

### Use something else when

- card: Each item needs an image, a summary, or free-form text — those are Cards.
- empty-state: There are no rows yet — that is an Empty state, in place of the body.

### Content rules

- Head columns with a noun in 10.5px caps — NAME, STATUS, OWNER — and never a sentence; the header is an index, not an explanation.
- Put the record's name in the second column and make it the widest: it is what the operator looks for before they read anything else.
- Write times as relative until they stop being useful — "2m ago", "6d ago" — and right-align them so the column scans as one measurement.
- Show status as a word in colour rather than a badge on every row: a column of badges is louder than the data and the rows stop being scannable.
- Keep the bulk toolbar's verbs to the three that are actually used often, and name them in caps as verbs — RUN, DUPLICATE, DELETE.

### Examples

- [demo] Automations
- [good] Few columns, each one a fact — Few columns, each one a fact used to decide; times right-aligned and relative.
- [bad] A column the operator can't read — Never keep a column the operator cannot read — if everything truncates, the extra columns belong in the row's detail.
- [good] Selection replaces the toolbar in place — A selection replaces the idle toolbar in place, counts what is selected, and keeps DELETE destructive.
- [bad] A second bar stacked for the selection — Never stack a second bar for the selection, and never let a destructive action pass as an ordinary one.
- [good] Actions reveal in a reserved column — Row actions appear on hover and focus in a reserved column, so the width never shifts.
- [bad] Every action spelled out on every row — Never spell every action out on every row — the rare ones belong in the row's overflow menu.

### Accessibility

- Real grid semantics: The body is a role="grid" with row and gridcell descendants and the header row marked columnheader, so a screen reader announces "row 4 of 214, Nightly ingest, Running" rather than reading a wall of unlabelled text.
- Nothing hover-only: Every action revealed on hover is reachable by tabbing into the row, and the actions column keeps its space at all times. An action that only exists under a pointer does not exist for half the operators.
- Selection is announced: Each box carries aria-checked and the count chip is a live region, so checking rows speaks "3 selected". The header box is a tri-state: none, some, all — and "some" is announced as mixed rather than as checked.
- Colour is never alone: Selection is the rail and the checked box as well as the ice tint, and status is a word rather than a colour. Ice on --panel measures 5.9:1; the tint alone is well under that and is never asked to carry meaning by itself.

### Tokens

- --panel-2: Toolbar band, row hover fill
- --accent-2: Selection rail, checked box, count chip
- --accent-2-line: Count chip border
- --accent: CREATE, running status, row triggers
- --border: Header hairline, card edge
- --border-2: Unchecked box, toolbar button borders
- --mute: Column names, row count
- --alarm-line, --alarm-soft: Destructive verbs' border and hover fill in the toolbar and row menu

### Related

- card (alternative): Use instead when each record needs more than a line — a summary, an image, a chart. Cards trade the scannable column for room to breathe.
- empty-state (composes-with): Replaces the body, never the toolbar, when there are no rows: the operator still needs CREATE and the column names to know what they are missing.
- popover (composes-with): The row's ⋯ menu is a popover, and it follows that component's rules — including keeping destructive rows under their own labelled divider.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Selection standardised on ice with a 2px rail; zebra striping ruled out; actions column reserved so rows never reflow.
- v1.0.1 (21 Aug 2026): Bulk toolbar swaps in place instead of stacking a second bar; header box made tri-state.
- v1.0.0 (15 Aug 2026): Table introduced with row selection, bulk actions and per-row overflow menus.

---

## Navigation (Tabs)

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 24 Aug 2026 · /components/tabs

Purpose: Switches between views of the page the operator is already on, with nothing else changing.

### Description

Tabs switch between views of the page the operator is already on.

Nothing about the page changes when a tab is clicked except which slice of it is showing: same route, same header, same object. That is the whole line against Navigation (Subnav) — a subnav row loads a different page, a tab re-dresses this one. The practical test is unsaved work: if moving between two views could lose it, they are tabs; if it could not, they were probably pages.

### Anatomy

1. Tab row — A single left-aligned row of labels with an 8px gap, sitting immediately above the content it governs. It never wraps, never scrolls and never centres — the first tab lines up with the page's left margin so the eye finds it without hunting.
2. Baseline — A 1px --border rule running the full width beneath the row. It is what makes the tabs read as a set rather than three loose words, and it is the rail the selected marker sits on.
3. Selected marker — A 2px --accent underline pulled 1px down so it covers the baseline exactly, paired with an --accent label. It moves over 160ms; nothing else in the row changes.
4. Tab label — Label type at 12px and .14em uppercase, in --mute at rest and --fg on hover, with 9px by 14px of padding to give a comfortable hit area. Hover deliberately stops short of the underline so it can never be mistaken for selection.
5. Panel — The view itself, on --panel-2 with the tab row's baseline as its top edge. It is the only thing that changes when a tab is clicked — the page header, title and actions above it hold still.

### Variants

- Page tabs (--accent, --mute, --fg, --border, --panel-2): The whole page has more than one shape — a fleet as a map or as a table. They sit directly under the page title, above everything else, because they govern all of it.
- Panel tabs (--accent, --mute, --fg, --border, --panel-2): One region of a page has alternate readings — a run's logs or its diff. Scoped to the card's header rail so the operator can see the tabs and the card's own edge belong together.

There is one style and it is the underline. No pill tabs — a filled rounded tab is a Chip, and the system will not spend the same shape twice. No vertical tabs, no closable tabs, no second row.

### States

- Default: --mute, no underline.
- Hover: --fg, still no underline.
- Selected: --accent + 2px underline.
- Focus: 3px accent-soft ring.

### Use when

- Two to five readings of the same object, all equally valid.
- Views the operator switches between often and compares against each other.
- Content that shares the page's header, title and actions unchanged.
- A split that can be thrown away without breaking a link, since tabs are not routes.

### Use something else when

- subnav: A different page — that is Navigation (Subnav).
- chip: A subset of one list — those are Chips above the table.

### Content rules

- Labels are Label case: one or two words, uppercase, .14em tracking — MAP, TABLE, LOGS, DIFF.
- Name the view, not the act: "MAP", never "VIEW MAP"; "DIFF", never "COMPARE VERSIONS".
- Keep every label in the row to a similar length; one long tab among three short ones makes the row look broken rather than emphasised.
- A count is allowed only when the number is the view's whole point — ALERTS 3 — set in --faint after the label, never as a coloured badge.
- Never put an action, a destination or Settings in a tab row. Everything in the row must be a way of looking at the same thing.

### Examples

- [demo] Page tabs
- [demo] Panel tabs
- [good] One row, underline only — One row, left aligned, underline on the selected tab and nothing else.
- [bad] Pill tabs — Never draw tabs as pills — that shape is a filter chip, and the operator will try to combine them.
- [good] Title stays put — The title stays put above the tabs, because the object is the same in every view.
- [bad] Overflow row with a destination — Never overflow or scroll a tab row, and never smuggle a destination like Settings into it.
- [good] Count in --faint — A count in --faint when the number is the view's whole point, sitting after the label.
- [bad] Coloured badge in a tab — Never put a coloured badge in a tab — the underline is the only mark a tab row carries.

### Accessibility

- Tablist and panel: The row is role="tablist", each label a role="tab" with aria-selected, and the view a role="tabpanel" labelled by its tab. That pairing is what lets a screen-reader user know how many views exist before choosing one.
- Arrows move, Tab leaves: Left and right arrows move between tabs and activate as they go; Home and End jump to the ends. One Tab press then lands in the panel, so reaching the content never means walking through every other tab.
- Colour is never alone: Selection is the 2px underline as well as the --accent label. Amber on --panel measures 6.6:1 and --mute labels 4.9:1 at 12px, but the underline is what carries the state for anyone who cannot separate the hues.
- Panel keeps its place: Switching a tab replaces the panel's content without moving focus or scrolling the page. The operator's position is preserved, and the change is announced by the panel's own heading rather than a live region.

### Tokens

- --accent: Selected label and 2px underline
- --mute, --fg: Resting and hover labels
- --border: Row baseline and panel edge
- --panel-2: Panel surface
- --faint: Optional count after a label

### Related

- subnav (often-confused-with): The subnav loads pages; tabs re-dress one. If the switch deserves its own URL and header, it belongs over there.
- chip (alternative): Chips filter the rows of one view and can combine. Tabs are exclusive and change the whole reading, which is why they never take the pill shape.
- card (composes-with): Panel tabs live in a card's header rail, so the card's edge and the tab baseline have to agree about where the content starts.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (24 Aug 2026): Pill tabs, overflow rows and badge counts ruled out; hover fixed at --fg with no underline.
- v1.0.1 (17 Aug 2026): Marker pulled 1px down so it covers the baseline instead of sitting above it.
- v1.0.0 (9 Aug 2026): Underline tabs introduced at two placements with a 160ms marker transition.

## Text

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/text

Purpose: Renders a block of copy in its role — eyebrow, heading, body or caption — with no typographic decision left to make at the point of use.

### Description

Text is two typefaces and four weights of grey, and every other typographic decision is already made.

Space Grotesk sets headings and numerals; IBM Plex Mono sets everything else, which is why this shell reads like an instrument rather than a document. There is no separate colour for emphasis: importance is carried by the grey ramp — --fg, --dim, --mute, --faint — and amber is reserved for things that act. Bold and italic are not part of the system.

### Anatomy

1. Eyebrow — An 11px --faint caps line at .2em tracking, above the heading. It carries the coordinates — which pipeline, which run — so the heading does not have to spend words locating itself.
2. Heading — Space Grotesk 600 with -.02em tracking, the only place the sans appears in a text block. Sentence case, one line, no full stop: it is a name, not a sentence.
3. Body — IBM Plex Mono at 14px on 1.6, set in --dim rather than --fg so the heading above it keeps its rank. Two or three lines at about a 70-character measure.
4. Emphasis — One step up the ramp to --fg for the clause that matters. This is the system’s entire emphasis vocabulary — no bold, no italic, no colour — so it can never compete with amber.
5. Caption — The smallest role, 11px --faint caps: timestamps, codes, counts. Its job is to be available rather than read, which is why it sits below everything and never above the heading.

### Variants

- Eyebrow (--mute): An 11px --faint caps line at .2em tracking, above the heading. It carries the coordinates — which pipeline, which run — so the heading does not have to spend words locating itself.
- Heading (--fg): Space Grotesk 600 with -.02em tracking, the only place the sans appears in a text block. Sentence case, one line, no full stop: it is a name, not a sentence.
- Body (--dim): IBM Plex Mono at 14px on 1.6, set in --dim rather than --fg so the heading above it keeps its rank. Two or three lines at about a 70-character measure.
- Caption (--mute): The smallest role, 11px --faint caps: timestamps, codes, counts. Its job is to be available rather than read, which is why it sits below everything and never above the heading.

### Use when

- One thing in a block matters more than the rest — move it up, not bigger.
- A line is supporting detail — --mute says so without shrinking it.
- The text is a machine fact nobody has to read — that is --faint.
- Two lines sit side by side and one is the answer — the ramp ranks them.

### Use something else when

- badge: The text is a system-assigned status — that is a Badge.
- button: The text acts when pressed — that is a Button or a link.
- empty-state: There is no content to describe — that is an Empty state.

### Content rules

- Write headings in sentence case with no terminal punctuation, and keep them to one line — a wrapping heading is a body paragraph that has not admitted it yet.
- Keep body paragraphs to three lines at a measure of roughly 70 characters. This shell is read while something is running; long copy will not be read at all.
- Reserve tracked caps for two or three words. Labels and captions only — a sentence in caps costs the reader more than the emphasis is worth.
- Set numbers in Grotesk with tabular figures wherever they stack, so a column of values lines up on the digit rather than drifting.
- Use the // prefix voice for machine asides in captions, and never for anything the operator is expected to act on.

### Examples

- [demo] Stack
- [demo] Eyebrow
- [demo] Heading
- [demo] Body
- [demo] Caption
- [good] Three steps down the ramp — Three steps down the ramp in one block: caption, heading, body. The hierarchy is colour, not size alone.
- [bad] A whole block at --fg — Never set a whole block at --fg — when everything is loudest, the block has no shape at all.
- [good] One clause, one step up — Emphasis inside a sentence is one step up the ramp, applied to the clause that matters.
- [bad] Amber or weight for emphasis — Never emphasise with amber or with weight — amber is for things that act, and there is no bold in this system.
- [good] Tracked label, Grotesk numeral — A label in tracked caps over a Grotesk numeral: the pattern every stat in the shell uses.
- [bad] A sentence in tracked caps — Never run a sentence in tracked caps — the tracking that makes two words legible makes ten words a wall.

### Accessibility

- The ramp is measured: --fg reads 15.8:1 on --bg, --dim 10.4:1 and --mute 5.7:1, all above the 4.5:1 body threshold. --faint measures 4.1:1, which is why it is restricted to 11px caps captions that repeat information available elsewhere.
- Size has a floor: Nothing below 10.5px, and nothing below 12px that carries information found nowhere else. The mono face buys legibility at small sizes but it does not buy an exemption.
- Structure, not styling: A heading is an h2 or h3 because of where it sits in the document, not because of its size. Type roles here are visual; the outline underneath them has to stand on its own.
- Colour is never alone: Error copy is --alarm and also says what is wrong in words; a struck-through line is also labelled complete. The ramp ranks importance — it never carries the meaning by itself.

### Tokens

- --fg: Headings, emphasis, values.
- --dim: Body copy, panel labels.
- --mute: Secondary lines, supporting detail.
- --faint: Captions, codes, timestamps.

### Related

- badge (often-confused-with): Differs in that a badge is a system-assigned status in a box. Coloured text is not a badge, and a badge is never a way to emphasise a word.
- button (contrasts-with): Where amber lives. If a run of text is amber and not inside a button or a link, something has taken the accent that should not have.
- card (composes-with): The container these roles are usually composed inside: eyebrow, heading, body, caption is the card’s stack in the order given here.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Numeral role documented as tabular Grotesk; bold and italic ruled out; body colour fixed at --dim.
- v1.0.1 (18 Aug 2026): --faint restricted to captions after contrast measurement; caption tracking raised to .2em.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Type system introduced — Space Grotesk for headings, IBM Plex Mono for everything else.

---

## Text input

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 2 Oct 2026 · /components/text-input

Purpose: One line the operator types into, and the box every other field in the system is measured against.

### Description

A text input is one line the operator types into, and the box every other field in the system is measured against.

Select, multi-select and textarea all inherit its border, radius, padding and height, so a form of mixed controls reads as one column of boxes rather than a collection of parts. It holds a value the operator authors, which is the line against every picker: if the legal answers are known in advance, hiding them behind free text is a trap. Anything longer than a line is a Textarea.

### Anatomy

1. Label — A 12px --dim caps line at .16em, always above the field and always present. It is never replaced by the placeholder, because the label has to survive the first keystroke.
2. Field — The reference box for the whole system: 10px/13px padding, 1px --border, 2px corner, --bg fill, 14px mono. Select, multi-select and textarea are this box with something added, never a box of their own.
3. Hint — One 11px --faint line stating the constraint before it is broken — casing, format, allowed characters. It occupies the same slot the error will, so the layout does not jump when validation fails.
4. Counter — An optional --faint count on the right of the hint row, shown only where a real limit exists. It counts up to the limit rather than down from it, so the number means the same thing as the value.
5. Error — Replaces the hint in #ff8f6b, naming what is wrong and what to type instead. The border turns with it, but the words are what the operator acts on — the colour is a locator.

### States

- Default: Empty and waiting. The placeholder is an example or an instruction in --mute, and it is never the only place the field says what it is.
- Filled: Holds a value. The border does not change on filling — only the text colour does, so a column of filled and empty fields still reads as one grid.
- Focus: Being typed into. The amber border plus the soft ring is the system focus treatment, and it is the one moment a field is allowed to be amber.
- Error: Failed validation, and only ever after the operator has finished — never while they are still typing the value that will pass.
- Disabled: Not editable now. The value stays readable and something adjacent says why; a field that cannot be typed into without explanation reads as broken.

There is no success state and no read-only variant distinct from disabled. A field that validated is simply a field with a value in it — a green tick on every correct answer teaches the operator to ignore the one that is wrong.

### Use when

- The operator authors the value and only they know it — a name, a key, a query.
- The answer is short enough to read back in one line.
- The legal answers cannot be listed in advance.
- Typing is genuinely faster than choosing, as it is in search.

### Use something else when

- select: The answers are a known list — that is a Select or a Radio group.
- textarea: The value runs past one line — that is a Textarea.
- checkbox: The answer is yes or no — that is a Checkbox or a Switch.

### Content rules

- Label every field with the noun it collects, in tracked caps above the box — and never let the placeholder take that job.
- Write the placeholder as an example of a good answer, not a repeat of the label: "nightly-ingest" beats "Enter pipeline name".
- State constraints in the hint before the operator types, so the error is a reminder rather than news.
- Write errors as a fact plus a fix — "Spaces are not allowed — try nightly-ingest" — and never as "Invalid input".
- Size the field to the answer: a retry count is 74px wide, a name is the column. The width is the first thing the operator reads.

### Examples

- [demo] Pipeline name
- [good] Persistent label and a stated constraint — A persistent label above and the constraint stated before the operator types.
- [bad] Placeholder standing in for the label — Never use the placeholder as the label — the first keystroke deletes the only clue what the field is.
- [good] An error with a fix — An error names what is wrong and offers the fix, in the same place the hint was.
- [bad] "Invalid input" — Never write an error the operator cannot act on — "Invalid input" is the border saying nothing twice.
- [good] Field width tracks the answer — Field width tracks the length of the answer, so the box itself says how much is expected.
- [bad] A one-character field at form width — Never stretch a one-character field to the form width — the box promises an essay and gets a digit.

### Accessibility

- Always a real label: Every field has a <label for> pointing at it — not an aria-label standing in for one, and never a placeholder doing the job. The visible label and the accessible name are the same words.
- Hints and errors are tied: The hint and the error are the same element, referenced by aria-describedby, so the constraint and the failure are announced with the field. On failure the input takes aria-invalid.
- Validation waits its turn: Validation runs on blur or submit rather than on every keystroke, because a field that announces an error mid-word talks over the operator typing the value that would have passed.
- Focus is visible and quiet: The soft amber ring measures 3px and is drawn outside the border, so it never shifts the layout. Amber on --bg reads 7.4:1, and the ring is present for pointer focus too — there is no focus-visible-only hiding here.

### Tokens

- --border: Resting field border
- --accent-line: Field border while focused
- --accent-soft: Focus ring
- --bg: Field fill
- --fg: Entered value
- --mute: Placeholder text
- --faint: Disabled value
- --mute: Hint and counter
- --alarm-line: Error border

### Related

- textarea (alternative): The same box grown a line taller and resizable vertically. Use it the moment the answer is a sentence rather than a value.
- select (alternative): Inherits this box exactly. If the legal answers are a known list, hiding them behind free text turns typing into guessing.
- button (composes-with): What commits the field. A text input never acts on its own — Enter submits the form, it does not run anything by itself.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Hint and error share one slot so validation never shifts the layout; success state ruled out; field width tied to answer length.
- v1.0.1 (17 Aug 2026): Validation moved to blur and submit; disabled value lightened to --faint at 55%.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Text input introduced as the reference box — 10px/13px padding, 2px corner, 14px mono.

---

## Textarea

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 2 Oct 2026 · /components/textarea

Purpose: The text input grown tall enough to hold a sentence the operator writes in their own words.

### Description

A textarea is the text input grown tall enough to hold a sentence the operator writes in their own words.

Border, radius, padding and type are inherited from Text input unchanged — only the height, the line-height and the resize handle are new, which is why the two never look like different components. Reach for it when the answer is prose: a note, a reason, a description. If the value is a name, a key or a number, the taller box is a promise the content will not keep.

### Anatomy

1. Label — The same 12px --dim caps line as every other field. A textarea is often the last question in a form, which is exactly when the label matters most — it is the one the operator reads after thinking.
2. Field — The input’s box with a 56px minimum height and 1.55 line-height, opening at about three lines. The height is the only promise the component makes about length, so it is set to the expected answer rather than to the maximum.
3. Handle — The native corner grip, vertical only. The operator can make room for a longer answer, but the box can never get wider than the column it sits in.
4. Hint — One 11px --faint line for the constraint — plain text, no formatting, what the note is for. It shares its slot with the error, so validation never moves the field.
5. Counter — The live count against the limit, right-aligned on the hint row. It is present from the first keystroke wherever a limit exists, and it turns with the message when the limit is passed.

### States

- Default: Empty, three lines tall. The empty height is the component’s only cue about how much is wanted, so it is chosen deliberately rather than left at the browser default.
- Filled: Holds prose. Line-height goes to 1.55 — the one measurement that differs from the input — because several lines of mono at 1.6 start to read as a paragraph rather than a field.
- Focus: Being written in. Identical to the input’s focus, and the field never scrolls or grows underneath the operator while they type.
- Error: Over the limit or missing when required. The counter turns with the border and the message says how much to cut, since “too long” without a number is not actionable.
- Disabled: Not editable now. The handle goes with it — a box that can still be resized but not typed into reads as a bug rather than a restriction.

The handle is vertical only, and there is no auto-growing variant. A box that resizes itself while the operator types moves the buttons under their cursor, and a box that resizes horizontally breaks the one column of boxes every form here is built on.

### Use when

- The answer is a sentence or two in the operator’s own words.
- Line breaks are part of the meaning — a note, a list, a pasted log.
- What is written will be read back later, by a person.
- The operator may want to see the whole answer at once before submitting.

### Use something else when

- text-input: The answer is a value on one line — that is a Text input.
- select: The answers are a known list — that is a Select.

### Content rules

- Set the opening height to the answer you expect, about three lines. A taller box asks for an essay; a one-line box tells the operator to be brief when they should not be.
- Write the placeholder as an example of a useful note, never as the label repeated — and never as the only statement of what the field is for.
- Show the counter from the first keystroke wherever a limit exists, counting up to the limit, and never let the limit arrive as a surprise.
- Say what the note is for in the hint — who reads it, whether it is kept — because prose is only worth writing if the operator knows where it goes.
- Never accept formatting the field cannot render. If markdown or headings are needed, the answer is an editor and not a taller box.

### Examples

- [demo] Why it was skipped
- [good] Three lines of room — Three lines of room for a two-line answer, with the limit shown from the start.
- [bad] A one-line textarea — Never ship a one-line textarea — if the answer will not fit, the operator writes less than they meant to.
- [good] A vertical-only handle — A vertical-only handle in the corner: the operator can make room, and the column stays intact.
- [bad] Resized wider than the form — Never allow horizontal resize — one box wider than the rest breaks the column every form is read down.
- [good] The counter turns over the limit — Over the limit, the counter turns with the message and says how much to cut.
- [bad] Keystrokes swallowed at the limit — Never swallow keystrokes at the limit with no counter — the operator thinks the field is broken.

### Accessibility

- Labelled like any field: A real <label for> and an aria-describedby pointing at the hint or error, exactly as the text input does. The taller box does not change the contract, and the label is never a placeholder.
- The counter is spoken: The count is a polite live region, so an operator who cannot see it hears how much room is left rather than discovering the limit when keystrokes stop landing.
- Tab leaves the field: Tab moves to the next control and Enter inserts a newline — the reverse of the input, and the reason a textarea is never the last thing before an implicit submit.
- Resize is not the only way: The handle is a convenience: the field scrolls its content and the value is never truncated visually without the counter saying so, so nothing depends on a drag a keyboard cannot perform.

### Tokens

- --border: Resting field border
- --accent-line: Field border while focused
- --accent-soft: Focus ring
- --bg: Field fill
- --border-2: Resize handle grip
- --faint: Disabled value
- --mute: Hint and counter
- --alarm-line: Error border

### Related

- text-input (composes-with): The box this inherits. Everything except height, line-height and the handle is documented there, and any change to the input changes this too.
- modal (composes-with): Where a long note usually belongs. A textarea inline in a dense panel is a hint the task deserved its own surface.
- button (composes-with): What commits the note. Enter is a newline here, so the submit has to be a real button rather than an implicit one.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Resize locked to vertical; auto-grow ruled out; counter required wherever a limit exists.
- v1.0.1 (17 Aug 2026): Minimum height set to 56px and line-height to 1.55; disabled state now disables the handle.
- v1.0.0 (11 Aug 2026): Textarea introduced as the text input with three lines of room.

---

## Toast

Status: stable · Version: 1.1.0 · Updated: 25 Aug 2026 · /components/toast

Purpose: A transient message reporting that something just happened. It says so once and leaves.

### Description

A toast reports what just happened, in the corner, and leaves on its own.

It is the cheapest surface in the system: it takes no focus, blocks nothing, and asks for nothing. That is also its limit — anything the operator must read or answer cannot be a toast, because it will be gone in 3.2 seconds and it was never in their way. A decision belongs in a Modal; a standing condition belongs in the panel that owns it, not in a corner that empties itself.

### Anatomy

1. Surface — A 320px --bg card with a hairline in the intent colour, docked to the top right under the header and sliding in over 180ms. It sits on --bg rather than --panel so it reads as being in front of the workspace without a shadow doing the work.
2. Rail — A 2px bar down the left edge in the intent colour. This is the intent, and the only place it is allowed to be a fill: two pixels of colour is enough to sort four kinds of message at a glance.
3. Title — The outcome in 14px --fg, past tense, five to seven words: “Workflow approved”, “Run failed”. If the operator reads nothing else, this line has to be the whole message.
4. Dot — A 7px disc in the intent colour beside the title, repeating what the rail says. It is deliberate redundancy: the rail is easy to miss at the edge of vision, and colour must never be the only carrier.
5. Detail — One 11.5px --mute line for the consequence — counts, durations, what happens next. Optional, never more than a line, and never the place the actual news lives.

### Variants

- Success (--accent, --accent-line): Something the operator asked for finished. Amber, because success here means an action completed — this is the one report that shares the acting colour.
- Fail (--alarm, --alarm-line): Something stopped and will not finish. It does not auto-dismiss, and it may carry one amber link to where the operator can look — never a decision.
- Info (--accent-2, --accent-2-line): A fact the system wants on the record: a schedule, a queue position, a sweep. Ice, because it refers to something rather than acting on it.
- Neutral (--mute, --border): A routine confirmation with no colour claim at all — saved, copied, closed. Most toasts should be this one; reaching for a colour is a decision, not a default.

There is no Warning intent, for the same reason there is no warning badge: a caution nobody has to act on is noise, and one they do have to act on is a failure or a modal. Intent is carried by a 2px rail and a dot — never by a filled background, which would make a corner report louder than the work behind it.

### Use when

- Something finished and the operator would otherwise not know.
- The outcome is worth a sentence but not worth their attention.
- The result arrived out of band — a background run, a sync, a queue.
- Missing the message costs nothing, because the state is legible elsewhere.

### Use something else when

- modal: The operator has to decide something — that is a Modal.
- callout: The message must survive being missed — that belongs in the panel that owns the state.
- badge: It annotates a row or a field — that is a Badge or an inline error.
- progress: Work is still running — that is Progress, which stays until it finishes.

### Content rules

- Write the title as an outcome in the past tense — “Workflow approved”, not “Approving workflow” or “Success!”. The event already happened; that is why there is a toast.
- Name the object, not the operation: “3 runs exported” beats “Export complete”, because the number is what the operator was actually waiting on.
- Keep the detail line to one clause of consequence, and drop it entirely when the title already says everything.
- Never put a question, a form, or two competing actions in a toast. One link to somewhere the operator can look is the maximum.
- Collapse repeats of the same event into one counted message rather than firing a second toast — the count is the news the second time.

### Examples

- [demo] Fire one
- [demo] Four intents
- [good] Outcome, consequence, rail — Outcome in the title, the consequence underneath, and a rail carrying the intent.
- [bad] A filled surface — Never fill the surface with the intent colour — a corner report outshouting the workspace is a lie about its importance.
- [good] A failure with one link — A failure may carry one amber link to where the operator can look — and it does not auto-dismiss.
- [bad] A question in a toast — Never ask a question in a toast — it takes no focus and leaves on a timer, so the answer is whatever the timeout chose.
- [good] A counted repeat — Repeats of the same event collapse into one counted toast rather than a stack.
- [bad] The same event, stacked — Never stack past three, and never repeat one event — a column of toasts is a queue nobody asked to read.

### Accessibility

- Announced, never focused: The container is an aria-live region — polite for success, info and neutral, assertive for failures — and focus never moves into it. A toast that steals focus takes the operator out of the field they were typing in.
- The timer is not the only way: Auto-dismiss is 3.2s, paused on hover and on keyboard focus anywhere inside, and failures do not dismiss at all. Anything that matters after the timer is also legible in the panel that owns it.
- Colour is never alone: Intent is the rail, the dot and the words together — “Run failed” says what the colour says. Salmon on --bg measures 6.2:1 and ice 5.9:1, but neither is asked to carry the meaning by itself.
- Dismiss is reachable: The ✕ is a real button labelled “Dismiss”, 26px and reachable by Tab while the toast is up. Escape clears the whole stack, so a keyboard operator is never stuck waiting out a timer.

### Tokens

- --bg: Toast surface
- --accent, --accent-line: Success rail and dot, action links
- --accent-2, --accent-2-line: Info rail and dot
- --mute: Neutral rail, detail line, dismiss glyph
- --border: Neutral hairline
- --fg: Title
- --alarm, --alarm-line: Fail rail, dot and hairline

### Related

- modal (often-confused-with): Where anything that needs an answer goes. The test is simple: if the message would be a problem to miss, it was never a toast.
- progress (composes-with): Covers the time before the toast. Progress stays while work runs; the toast is the one line that reports how it ended.
- badge (alternative): Where a standing condition belongs. A toast reports a transition once; a badge keeps saying what is true.

### Changelog

- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Warning intent ruled out; failures no longer auto-dismiss; repeats collapse into one counted toast.
- v1.0.1 (20 Aug 2026): Filled backgrounds replaced by the 2px rail and dot; stack capped at three.
- v1.0.0 (13 Aug 2026): Toast introduced top right at 320px with a 3.2s dismiss.

---

## Tooltip

Status: stable · Version: 1.2.0 · Updated: 19 Sept 2026 · /components/tooltip

Purpose: Names the thing under the pointer, in one line, and holds nothing the operator has to reach.

### Description

A tooltip names the thing under the pointer, in one line, and holds nothing the operator has to reach.

It exists so an icon can stay an icon. Because it appears on hover and takes no pointer events, everything inside it is unreachable by definition — no links, no buttons, no selectable text. That is the whole line against Popover: the moment content has to be clicked, the trigger has to be clicked too. And a tooltip never carries information that exists nowhere else, because a pointer is one of several ways to use this shell.

### Anatomy

1. Bubble — A --bg box with an --accent-line hairline and a soft drop shadow, fading in over 160ms. Amber on the border rather than a fill: the bubble belongs to the control the operator is already pointing at, and it is gone the moment they are not.
2. Label — One line of 12px --fg with white-space:nowrap — the bubble is as wide as the sentence and never wraps. If the text cannot survive that constraint, it is not tooltip content.
3. Offset — 9px between trigger and bubble. Enough that the bubble reads as a separate surface, close enough that the pairing is unambiguous, and small enough that the pointer never crosses it — there is nothing to cross to.
4. Trigger — The control being named, usually an icon-only button. It owns the hover, keeps its own focus ring, and the tooltip never covers it — the bubble flips sides rather than sitting on top of what it describes.

### States

- Top by default: Every tooltip opens above its trigger, centred. One default side means a row of icons produces a predictable line of bubbles rather than a scatter.
- Flips when clipped: Against the top of the viewport it goes below; against a side it goes left or right. It flips rather than shifts, so the 9px relationship to the trigger is never stretched.
- Never covers the trigger: The bubble is not allowed to sit over the control it names. An operator checking what something is should not lose sight of the thing itself.
- No pointer events: The bubble cannot be hovered, clicked or selected, which is what makes it safe to appear under the cursor — and what makes any interactive content inside it a bug.
- Delay in, none out: A 400ms wait before showing, so crossing a toolbar does not flash five bubbles; instant hide on leave, so nothing lingers over work.
- One at a time: Only one tooltip exists at once, and moving between triggers inside 400ms swaps its content rather than re-running the delay.

There is no arrow, no title row, and no rich variant. The 9px offset and the amber hairline are enough to tie the bubble to its trigger, and anything that needed a heading was never one line long.

### Use when

- An icon-only control needs its name spelled out.
- A truncated cell needs its full value on demand.
- A keyboard shortcut is worth showing next to the control it fires.
- The information is a convenience — the operator can work without ever seeing it.

### Use something else when

- popover: Anything inside has to be clicked — that is a Popover.
- text-input: The text explains a field's constraint — that is the field's own hint line.
- toast: It reports something that just happened — that is a Toast.

### Content rules

- Write the control’s name, in sentence case, with no full stop: "Duplicate run". It is a label, not a sentence.
- Keep it under about six words. Anything longer belongs in the layout, where every operator can read it.
- Append the shortcut after a middot where one exists — "Duplicate run · D" — so the tooltip teaches the faster path.
- Never repeat text already visible next to the control; a tooltip on a labelled button is noise on every hover.
- Never put a constraint, a reason or a warning in a tooltip. If the operator needs it to act correctly, it cannot be hidden behind a pointer.

### Examples

- [demo] Demo
- [good] Name and shortcut, one line — The control's name, and its shortcut, on one line above the icon.
- [bad] Paragraph and a link — Never put a paragraph or a link in a tooltip — it takes no pointer events, so the link cannot be reached.
- [good] Constraint in the hint line — A field's constraint lives in its hint line, where it is readable before the operator types.
- [bad] Constraint behind a question mark — Never hide a rule behind a question mark — a constraint discoverable only by hovering is a constraint most operators will break.
- [good] Full value on hover — A truncated value gets its full text on hover — the one case where the tooltip repeats what is already on screen.
- [bad] Repeats a visible label — Never label a control that is already labelled — a tooltip repeating visible text is noise on every hover.

### Accessibility

- Never the only copy: Because a tooltip needs a pointer and a wait, nothing in it is load-bearing. Every icon-only control also carries a real accessible name, and every rule it might state is written in the layout.
- Described, not labelled: The bubble is role="tooltip" tied to its trigger with aria-describedby, so it is heard as extra description after the control’s own name rather than replacing it.
- Keyboard shows it too: Focusing the trigger shows the tooltip with no delay and Escape dismisses it, so a keyboard operator gets the same hint a pointer does — hover is not the only path.
- Nothing to chase: With pointer-events off and a 0ms hide, there is no bubble to move the cursor into and nothing that can be lost by moving too slowly — the failure mode of hoverable tooltips.

### Tokens

- --bg: Bubble surface.
- --accent-line: Bubble hairline.
- --fg: Label text.
- --border-2: Trigger border.
- --panel-2: Trigger fill.

### Related

- popover (often-confused-with): Where anything clickable goes. The test is the pointer: if the operator has to reach into it, the trigger has to be a click.
- main-rail (composes-with): Its most common production trigger: every icon in the collapsed rail names itself with a Tooltip instead of a native title.
- text-input (contrasts-with): Owns field constraints. A rule about what may be typed belongs in the hint line under the field, never behind a question mark.
- button (composes-with): The usual trigger. An icon-only button needs both a tooltip for the pointer and an accessible name for everything else.

### Changelog

- v1.2.0 (19 Sept 2026): Adopted by the collapsed main rail — icon-only rows and the collapse/expand toggle now use this component in place of a native title.
- v1.1.0 (25 Aug 2026): Arrow and rich variant ruled out; 400ms in / 0ms out fixed; single-instance swap documented.
- v1.0.1 (19 Aug 2026): Bubble flips instead of shifting when clipped; keyboard focus now shows it without delay.
- v1.0.0 (12 Aug 2026): Tooltip introduced above the trigger at a 9px offset with no pointer events.

## Usage card

Status: stable · Version: 1.0.0 · Updated: 1 Oct 2026 · /components/usage-card

Purpose: The paired "use when / use something else when" card on a docs page. Not an operator-facing component outside documentation.

### Description

A Usage Card states a rule in two halves — where a component belongs, and where it doesn't.

It exists so a doc page can draw its own boundary in one glance, instead of burying it in a paragraph. That is the line against Callout: a callout reports one live fact with an icon, this card states a standing rule with none. It is documentation furniture, not a product surface — no screen outside this reference site renders one, at least for now.

### Anatomy

1. Pair — Always two, side by side, never one alone — the belongs-here card only means something next to its opposite.
2. Title — 11px uppercase at .2em: "Use when" / "Reach for X when" on the left, "Use something else when" on the right, always in that order.
3. Rows — A plain list of full sentences, 13.5px --dim, 9px gap, no bullets or numbers — each row is one condition, not a fragment.
4. Frame — Left card gets --accent-line border and --accent-soft fill; right card gets a plain --border-2 border and no fill. Colour marks which side is the recommendation.

### Use when

- A doc page needs to draw a hard boundary against its nearest neighbour.
- The rule has a real opposite worth naming, not just a definition to restate.

### Use something else when

- callout: The fact is live and momentary, not a standing rule — that is a Callout.

### Content rules

- The left title always names the affirmative case in the page’s own words ("Use when", "Reach for amber when") — never a generic "Do".
- The right title is always the fixed phrase "Use something else when" and always names the correct component inline, in --fg, inside the sentence.
- Each row is a complete condition an operator could actually be facing, not a restated definition of the component itself.
- Row count does not have to match between the two sides — the right side is often shorter, because ruling something out takes fewer words than justifying it.
- Never a single card. If there is nothing to rule out, the usage rule belongs in prose in the opening description instead.

### Examples

- [demo] Pair
- [good] Custom recommendation title — The left title narrows to the page’s own words ("Reach for amber when") instead of the generic default — Content rule 1.
- [bad] A single card alone — One card with nothing to rule out reads as unfinished — a standalone rule like this belongs in prose in the opening description instead (Content rule 5).

### Accessibility

- Not interactive: Neither card is a control — no focus ring, no onClick, no tabIndex. It is read, not operated.
- Colour never alone: The recommended side carries the amber border and fill together; a colour-blind reader still gets the left/right position and the title text.
- Reading order matches DOM order: The recommended card is always first in markup as well as on screen, so a screen reader hears the affirmative case before the exclusions.
- Component names are real links: Where the right card names another component inline, that word should be reachable, not just coloured — treat it the way Related treats its cards.

### Tokens

- --accent-line, --accent-soft: Recommended card: border and fill.
- --border-2: Alternative card: border, no fill.
- --accent, --mute: Title colour, left vs. right.
- --dim: Row text.
- --fg: A named component inline in a row.

### Related

- callout (often-confused-with): The nearest neighbour by look, not by job. A callout has an icon and reports one live fact; this card has no icon and states a standing rule.
- card (composes-with): The plain bordered box this pattern is built from. Usage Card is a fixed, paired arrangement of that box — never a variant registered on Cards itself.

### Changelog

- v1.0.0 (1 Oct 2026): Documented as its own component — this pattern already appeared, identically, on every Foundations and Components doc page.
